entries.title: White Sox Pope Leo night draws out thousands for pope hats and Catholic fanfare
entries.summary: <p>Cynthia Castañeda has been Catholic as long as she’s been a White Sox fan — for her entire life.</p><p>Despite clear weather after severe storms that could only be described as an act of God, she and her husband Michael made the trip from Indiana to make the game and, more importantly, to celebrate Pope Leo XIV.</p><p>They were among the tens of thousands lining up outside Guaranteed Rate Field who collected a complementary Sox-themed pope hat.</p><p>The couple, who both grew up on the South Side, are hoping the Sox-loving pope's presence could bring about a new championship era.</p><p>“It makes for a deeper connection knowing he’s a Sox fan,” she said. “I hope he’s back for another World Series win.”</p><p>The giveaway was initially intended for just 2,500 fans with special tickets. But the giveaway soon expanded to the entire stadium of nearly 41,000.</p><p>As for making the pope-themed game an annual tradition? </p><p>“We’ll see,” says Brooks Boyer, White Sox executive vice president. “We wanna be super respectful to the pope, to the Vatican. Hopefully this represents a tie to his childhood team, doing it the exact right way.”</p><p>Vendors outside the stadium sold pope pins, hats and shirts bearing the classic Sox batter logo adorning the papal crown.</p><p>The hats weren’t the game's only religious fare.</p><p>Famed former White Sox organist Nancy Faust returned to her seat to perform the National Anthem after the first pitch was thrown out by Sister Mary Jo Sobieck of the Dominican Sisters of Springfield. </p><p>It was Sobieck’s second time at the mound. In 2018, she <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-saturday/2019/7/6/20684123/espy-2019-award-nominee-sister-mary-jo-white-sox-strike" target="_blank" ><u>grabbed headlines tossing heat</u></a> across the plate for another ceremonial first pitch.</p><p>The pregame ceremony included the handover of an oversize check totaling $14,000 to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2024/06/04/augustinian-catholic-order-clergy-sex-abuse-richard-mcgrath" target="_blank" ><u>Midwest Augustinian Province</u></a>, the order to which <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/05/09/pope-leo-cardinal-robert-prevost-midwest-augustinians-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>then-Fr. Robert Prevost once belonged</u></a>. Students from Our Lady of Mount Carmel Academy’s kids’ conclave joined players on the field briefly.</p><p>Preceding the seventh inning stretch, the team held a fifth inning “Peace be with you,” led by Evergreen Park and Marist High School alum Father Tom Hurley and comedian Pat McGann.</p><p>Not everyone was there for His Holiness.</p><p>Michael Rodriguez, a lifelong Sox fan, arrived with loved ones to celebrate his 29th birthday.</p><p>Rodriguez called it “God’s will” that the game landed the day before his birthday and brought him back to the stadium for the first time in five years.</p><p>“Growing up I was able to see the fireworks from my house in Pilsen, and it was always a great feeling,” Rodriguez said. “It still makes my face light up.”</p><p>Rodriguez credits the team’s recent success on the magic wand they've been waving from the dugout, not the pontiff. But the team really found what it needed in the recent trade for pitcher Luis Castillo, he said.</p><p>“I grew up in the World Series run, and that was magic to me,” Rodriguez said. “This team seems like they could make a magical run.”</p><p><i>Contributing: Jeff Agrest</i></p>

entries.title: 2 tornadoes packing winds of 86 to 110 mph hit Chicago area, toppling trees and leaving 250,000 without power
entries.summary: <p>Two tornadoes hit the Chicago area on Tuesday in a fast-moving storm with 99 mph winds that left a path of destruction in the south suburbs and cut power to hundreds of thousands.</p><p>The National Weather Service said two tornadoes with gusts of 86 to 110 mph hit southern Cook County, on its border with Will County, and in eastern Will County.</p><p>Survey teams continued working to confirm possible tornadoes near Homer Glen, Tinley Park, Crete and Manhattan — just weeks after surveyors confirmed <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/30/seven-7-confirmed-tornadoes-weather-service-illinois-monday-storms" target="_blank" >seven tornadoes hit</a> the south and west suburbs in a different storm.</p><p>The storms also damaged parts of Chicago. entries.title: Man seriously injured in Englewood shooting
entries.summary: <p>A man was seriously injured in a shooting in Englewood Tuesday night, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The man, 36, was sitting near the sidewalk in the 7300 block of South Union Avenue around 6:15 p.m. when multiple people approached him and at least one fired shots, police said in a statement. He was shot several times and taken to University of Chicago Medical Center in serious condition.</p><p>No one is in custody, police said.</p>

entries.title: White Sox give 2B Chase Meidroth more time to rest ailing wrist
entries.summary: <p>White Sox second baseman Chase Meidroth wasn’t in the lineup for the second consecutive game Tuesday because of a sore left wrist. He said he hurt it on a swing in the game Friday and the pain got progressively worse, but the soreness had been lingering for weeks.</p><p>“It’s something to nip in the bud,” Meidroth said before the opener of a three-game series against the Reds. “Off day yesterday, get another one today and see how it feels tomorrow. We’ve got a long stretch coming up, so we felt it was good to get ahead of it right now.”</p><p>The game was the first in a stretch of 16 games in 16 days, thanks to a makeup game Aug. 20 against the Braves removing a day off.</p><p>Meidroth took infield before the game, wearing a brace that he said holds the tendon on the back of his wrist in place and takes pressure off of it. He said an MRI exam came back clean and he took a cortisone shot the other day.</p><p>“There was no fracture and no hamate [issue],” manager Will Venable said. “It’s going to be a pain-tolerance thing, and he’s not going to put himself in more danger. But we’ve got to be mindful of where he’s at and give him another day.”</p><p>Whenever the lingering soreness began, Meidroth hasn’t let it affect his hitting. In 20 games since the All-Star break, Meidroth is slugging .529. In 93 games before the break, he slugged .379. Of his 11 home runs this season, four have come since the break, including two blasts Thursday.</p><p>“Just continuing to work,” Meidroth said of his increased slug, which has been on a roller coaster and is up to .404 for the season. “Again, I can’t say enough good things about our hitting staff in helping me all year and getting me to this point. The ups and downs are part of every season. Obviously, it was good last week.”</p><p>“Chase is such a tough guy, and he wants to be out there,” Venable said. “This isn’t the first ailment that he’s had that he’s played well through. It’s impressive that he’s gotten off some really good swings with a hand that’s bothering him.”</p><h3>Giving Colson a break</h3><p>Sometimes the reason behind a baseball decision isn't analytical at all.</p><p>Venable has said he will use Randal Grichuk, Munetaka Murakami, Miguel Vargas and Colson Montgomery as the DH against left-handers. On Tuesday, he chose Montgomery against Reds lefty Nick Lodolo. Why?</p><p>“Colson hit a homer the other day when he DH’d, so why not?" Venable said.</p><p>“But also with him physically, especially starting this 16-game stretch, with the foul balls off his legs, I think there’s still some soreness in there. So just want to be mindful of that, make sure that we’re protecting him.”</p><h3>Burke bounces back</h3><p>Right-hander Sean Burke recovered from a subpar outing last week in Boston, allowing the Reds one run and three hits in seven innings, one out shy of his season high. He struck out eight and didn’t walk anyone.</p><p>Burke’s ERA had dropped in eight consecutive outings until last Wednesday, when he allowed two runs in 4 ⅓ innings against the Red Sox. He found his form Tuesday, holding the Reds hitless until Eugenio Suarez’s leadoff homer in the fifth.</p><h3>Notes</h3><p>Right-hander Davis Martin will start the series finale against the Reds on Thursday. He’ll pitch on three days of rest because he threw just one inning Sunday against the Guardians before a rain delay ended his day.</p><p>• Catcher Kyle Teel, who’s recovering from a sprained left ankle, looked good running in the outfield before the game and said he’s feeling much better. He’s still likely weeks from returning.</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a entries.title: Indiana Fever coach Stephanie White says divisiveness 'will not win'
entries.summary: <p>INDIANAPOLIS — Indiana Fever coach Stephanie White has had enough of the conversations around the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/wnba" >WNBA</a> this season that aren't about basketball.</p><p>On Tuesday, she finally lashed out.</p><p>The 2023 WNBA Coach of the Year and one of the original Fever players angrily defended herself after she was criticized for her response to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" >Sky</a> player DiJonai Carrington's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/08/08/dijonai-carrington-ejected-after-hard-foul-on-sophie-cunningham-as-sky-fall-to-fever" >flagrant foul on Sophie Cunningham,</a> and pleaded with people to focus on the sport and not the continual sideshows.</p><p>"The hate, the fear mongering, the divisiveness that's trying to hijack our league will not win. It won't win," White said, her voice rising as she pounded the table in front of her. "We are united. We are connected. We will not be divided. Every day these women put their ass on the line. Every day when they go low, we go high. Love will win. Grace will win. Humility will win and kindness will win. I stand by them, I will always stand by them. Everybody else can go to hell."</p><p>White left immediately after her 2½-minute outburst ended without taking questions.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Stephanie White made the following statement before tonight's game: <a href="https://t.co/VkYThRldsu">pic.twitter.com/VkYThRldsu</a></p>— Indiana Fever (@IndianaFever) <a href="https://x.com/IndianaFever/status/2087318100253221000?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 11, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>For the Fever, this has been a season full of controversies.</p><p>It happened again Saturday when Carrington hit Cunningham in the head and neck area, knocking the Fever guard hard to the ground on a breakaway layup. Cunningham got up and charged toward Carrington but was restrained.</p><p>Carrington was assessed a Flagrant 2, an automatic ejection. The Sky player then wrote "WHITE PRIVILEGE" and tagged the Fever on a social media account. On Monday, Carrington said she never claimed the foul call was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/08/10/dijonai-carrington-says-white-privilege-post-goes-beyond-flagrant-foul" >“white privilege.”</a></p><p>Cunningham has been outspoken about her desire to keep transgender women out of women's sports, a position that has spurred rallies in support of and opposed to her stance.</p><p>White initially said she thought the refs got the call right but that she didn't think that action near the head and neck area was intentional. Critics claimed she was defending Carrington.</p><p>""OK. ... The Indiana Fever need to let Stephanie White go," Indiana Lieutenant Gov. Micah Beckwith wrote Sunday on X. "No solid coach would ever take the side of the opposing team's player who committed a flagrant foul on one of your own players. Terrible coaching! The Fever need to defend their players."</p><p>White explained Tuesday that she had not seen the replay when she first spoke with reporters Saturday and that she changed her opinion after watching it again. She called the foul "egregious."</p><p>"Our players' success, our players' health and wellness, our players' safety is always a top priority," she began, her voice rising. "One of the things I pride myself on is my relationships with my players. For those who have anything to say about the play in the last game, I didn't see the replay. I went straight to a press conference, I thought the play got called right. Thankfully, Sophie is OK. Was it egregious? Absolutely.</p><p>"When you get a chance to see that on replay over and over, you see that. I didn't see that in real time. I personally take any suggestions that I don't 100% always have my players back. I ride with them 10 toes down all the time, all the time."</p><p>Cunningham received a loud ovation when she entered Tuesday's game against the New York Liberty. White received polite applause when she was introduced.</p><p>White faced a similar controversy when three-time All-Star Caitlin Clark also was fouled hard earlier this season, prompting a letter from the U.S. House of Representatives to WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert.</p><p>White and Clark also were involved in a sideline spat in late and there was speculation about White's job status following the incident.</p><p>Now White just wants everyone to get back to basketball.</p><p>"It's a shame we can't have an opportunity to talk about what great basketball they are playing," White said with emphasis. "The reality is, with me, I will always lead with love. I will always lead with grace, I will always lead with humility. and I will always lead with integrity. It doesn't mean I'll always get it right. I'm human."</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" entries.title: Former charter operator Aspira declares bankruptcy, could keep profit from sale of taxpayer-funded building
entries.summary: <p>On a busy stretch of North Milwaukee Avenue, the four-story windows of a sleek white limestone building are devoid of activity just weeks before the start of school.</p><p>The state spent $27 million to build the former charter school just over a decade ago. But instead of getting ready to welcome back students, the Avondale building is on the verge of being sold to a real-estate investment company for a fraction of what taxpayers spent to construct it.</p><p>The charter school’s former operator, Aspira Inc. of Illinois, recently filed for bankruptcy, after it was forced to close two schools in March, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/02/26/cps-to-shut-down-financially-distressed-aspira-campuses-scattering-students-to-new-schools" target="_blank" ><u>leaving more than 500 students to transfer midyear</u></a>. In bankruptcy court filings, the nonprofit cited the loss of funding from Chicago Public Schools and “significant and continuing financial distress.”</p><p>The situation raises questions about whether Aspira will be able to pocket money from the sale of its taxpayer-funded building to pay for its own operations. It’s also unclear whether CPS or the state will be able to recoup anything from the sale<b> </b>after sending millions to Aspira.</p><p>Aspira officials have indicated in court documents that they want to sell the Milwaukee building and use the money to pay off debts and keep operating in some capacity.</p><p>Interim executive director, Melissa Batista, noted that Aspira still operates a public alternative high school within CPS that reenrolls dropouts and runs youth development and community engagement programming at the Aspira Community Center.</p><p>“Looking ahead, our focus is on rebuilding and rebranding ASPIRA while returning to the organization’s roots focused on education, youth leadership, and service to our communities,” she wrote in a statement on Tuesday. “There are significant challenges in front of us, but there is also an opportunity to rebuild with intention.”</p><p>When the state gave Aspira money to construct its building on Milwaukee Avenue, officials praised the community organization’s commitment “to the self-determination of Latino and other underserved youth.”</p><p>Now, Iris Martinez, the former Democratic state senator who helped Aspira obtain the grants from Springfield, said the situation is “a disaster all the way around.” Martinez blamed Aspira administrators and board members but said she doesn’t see any way for the state to claw back its investment.</p><p>“To see that today the school sits there right now empty, with the possibility of it being bought off by a developer who probably will convert it into condos — that to me is a heartbreak,” Martinez said.</p><p>A spokesperson for the Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity, which awarded the grants to Aspira, said Tuesday that agency officials are looking into the matter after questions from WBEZ.</p><p>Meanwhile, Aspira’s contract with CPS, like all the district’s charter contracts, specifies that if Aspira ceases to operate its schools, the organization “shall” return “any property or assets” used to run its schools that were purchased with CPS money. State law seeks to clear up any ambiguity by saying that anything “purchased with public funds shall be returned to the school district” from which the charter drew its enrollment.</p><p>Over the past decade, CPS sent $156 million to Aspira to run its charter schools, including $8 million in facility stipends for the Milwaukee Avenue building.</p><p>In the past, some have said CPS did not work hard enough to recoup assets from closed charters. Jen Conant, the charter division chair for the Chicago Teachers Union, said this time needs to be different, especially because CPS gave Aspira extra money every year to operate in non-CPS facilities.</p><p>“If CPS doesn’t recover the additional funds from the sale of the Milwaukee building, other charter operators will learn that they can open up a school and leverage public funds to do it, shut it down within a few years, and walk away with the taxpayer-funded real estate and capital for their own private purposes,” she said. “Public funds, public school dollars are for the education of our children, not for private operators to play with.”</p><p>Aspira officials did not answer questions about what they believe CPS is entitled to.</p><h3><b>Aspira’s buildings are worth millions, but where will that money go?</b></h3><p>Aspira’s most substantial assets are two Avondale buildings that housed high schools, court records show — the modern one on Milwaukee Avenue and another older building less than a mile away on West Barry Avenue that Aspira bought and renovated.</p><p>Court documents reveal that the two properties are tied together. The Barry Avenue property was appraised at $4.5 million — much less than Aspira officials thought it was worth. In an April resolution, board members cited that lower estimated value as one of the reasons they approved filing for bankruptcy.</p><p>Aspira still owes $5.4 million on a mortgage on the Barry Avenue property, court records show, and the organization intends to use proceeds from the Milwaukee Avenue sale to pay off that mortgage.</p><p>When Aspira put the Milwaukee Avenue building up for sale, <a class="Link" href="https://images1.showcase.com/d2/RutaJhL163YxVze3jesqELgIqTH9LQRuJ30-mKM00F4/document.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>the real-estate listing touted</u></a> that it remains in pristine condition, and has had “significant capital investment” that would “support continued use or seamless adaptive reuse.”</p><p>The building also is “LEED Gold Certified,” the listing states, meaning it meets high environmental and energy-efficiency standards.</p><p>It did not take long for Aspira to find a buyer. Last week, Aspira reported to the bankruptcy court that the organization had accepted a $11 million offer from Saxony Properties, LLC — a million dollars less than Aspira thought it would fetch. Aspira will go before the court on Aug. 25 to try to get approval for the sale.</p><p>The owner of Saxony Properties, which owns and rents dozens of North Side apartments, did not respond to a call and email asking what it plans to do with the building.</p><p>In court documents, Aspira says that $11 million is a “fair and reasonable” price and states that Saxony is not an insider and that the contract was negotiated at “arms length.”</p><p>Aspira indicated in court documents it would use profits from the sale of the Milwaukee Avenue “to satisfy creditor claims and fund the Debtor's operations or plan of reorganization.”</p><p>If Aspira is permitted to sell the building, the first debt it has to settle is the $5.4 million it owes to Old Second National Bank, which holds the mortgage on the Barry Avenue building. Next will be the real estate attorney, a former board president of Aspira, who will get $27,500.</p><p>Aspira provided the court with a long list of other debts that need to be satisfied. The Chicago Teachers Pension Fund, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Illinois, which handled Aspira staff’s health insurance, and a lending company called PEAC Solutions are each owed more than $200,000.</p><p>Edgar Lopez, the executive director who left after Aspira’s schools closed, believes he should get $240,000, but Aspira disputes that claim. Lopez did not return messages seeking comment.</p><p>Aspira also owes more than $54,000 to ComEd and nearly $26,000 to Peoples Gas.</p><p>Altogether, Aspira lists $1.5 million in unsecured claims that are not backed by property or other collateral.</p><p>CPS is on the list of Aspira’s creditors filed in court records, but, according to the bankruptcy documents, the debt to the school district is only around $2,700. The school district’s attorney has yet to appear in court on the matter or file a motion to intervene.</p><p>The bankruptcy court decides what happens once Aspira’s creditors are paid off. In addition to any leftover money from the Milwaukee Avenue building, Aspira has the Barry Avenue building and nearly 800 items in inventory, including numerous laptops, speakers, microscopes and school furniture.</p><h3><b>Some say Aspira’s situation points to need for more accountability</b></h3><p>No other charter school has filed for bankruptcy in Chicago and it is extremely rare for it to happen anywhere, though a few hundred close each year, according to the National Alliance for Public Charter Schools, a Washington D.C.- based advocacy organization.</p><p>Derek W. Black, a law professor at the University of South Carolina who has written extensively about charter schools, says many people don’t understand that charter schools get public funds but are mostly left to manage and spend their money as they want. Typically, he said, their assets “do not belong to the people of the state of Ohio or Illinois or New Jersey.”</p><p>And while some states have accountability measures that dictate what happens if a charter school closes, often, when an operator walks away, there isn’t much holding them accountable.</p><p>It raises questions like: “Who is looking out for the taxpayers?” Black said. “Who is looking out for the community?”</p><p>Lopez, Aspira’s former CEO, argued that the way CPS funds charter schools led to Aspira’s financial problems. He accused CPS of giving charter schools just 83% of what the district would typically spend per student, not the 97% required by state law.</p><p>He said the organization was doomed by that discrepancy, along with a drop in enrollment and an increase in the labor costs for unionized staff.</p><p>The Illinois Network of Charter Schools, a charter advocacy group, did not defend Aspira, but said in a statement that it expected the proper legal processes to be followed in the closure of the charter schools and the bankruptcy proceedings.</p><p>The group also echoed concerns that Chicago charter schools are being underfunded as they face many of the same enrollment and financial challenges as district-run schools.</p><p>But CPS officials contend that Aspira’s difficulties are unique.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/11/19/chicago-public-schools-aspira-charter-network-finances-cps-investigation" target="_blank" ><u>Last November, CPS told Aspira’s board</u></a> that a months-long district investigation allegedly found “a failure of governance” and “a lack of financial proficiency necessary to successfully run a school.”</p><p>When Lopez asked for a second cash advance in February, the Chicago School Board balked and then <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/03/19/cps-revokes-aspiras-ability-to-operate-charter-schools-in-chicago-in-rare-move-board-of-education" target="_blank" ><u>voted unanimously in March</u></a> to end its contract with Aspira — the only time the school district has revoked a charter in the middle of the school year.</p><p>WBEZ has been seeking information to get a better picture of what led to Aspira’s financial troubles. In March, WBEZ filed a Freedom of Information request with Aspira for payroll information, financial statements, audits and other public records.</p><p>Charter schools are subject to the state’s open-records law, but Aspira did not provide the requested records. Chicago Public Media sued Aspira in Cook County Circuit Court for access to those documents.</p><p>Aspira’s bankruptcy lawyer, Paul Bach, has asserted that the open-records case was automatically put on hold due to the bankruptcy filing. But lawyers for Chicago Public Media said they will challenge that.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/03/19/cps-revokes-aspiras-ability-to-operate-charter-schools-in-chicago-in-rare-move-board-of-education" >CPS revokes Aspira’s ability to operate charter schools in Chicago in rare move</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/02/26/cps-to-shut-down-financially-distressed-aspira-campuses-scattering-students-to-new-schools" >Caught in the middle: More than 500 students to be displaced by CPS shutdown of Aspira schools</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/03/05/aspira-will-soon-have-no-teachers-or-money-cps-is-still-struggling-to-close-it" >Aspira will soon have no teachers or money. CPS is still struggling to close it</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/11/25/cps-to-help-aspira-make-payroll-but-charter-operators-financial-woes-remain" >CPS to help Aspira make payroll, but charter operator’s financial woes remain</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/11/19/chicago-public-schools-aspira-charter-network-finances-cps-investigation" >CPS blasts longtime charter operator for alleged financial ‘negligence’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Matt Shaw still waiting for pain-free hand, loving Cubs in meantime: ‘Wow, this is a really good team’
entries.summary: <p>WASHINGTON — <b>Matt Shaw</b>’s sprained hand is still bugging him.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ utility man updated Tuesday that he’s “finally over that hump” and feeling better, but the team still has some markers for him to hit, some pain that still needs to go away before he can come back from an injured-list stay that’s lasted a month and a half.</p><p>“We’ve gotten to the point where I can swing almost full effort with no pain, or a little pain,” Shaw said. “If I can get to the point where I can swing and miss or take a funky swing, things like that, with no pain, if I can do that — or at least like a 1 or 2, low-level pain — that’s definitely the marker to be like, ‘OK, ready to go.’</p><p>“It’s been long. It’s felt like a really long time. I’m definitely getting antsy to be getting ready to play. But it’s been good watching the boys crushing it of late. I’m really excited to get back. I miss being out there. I miss all of it. I’m looking forward to it, for sure.”</p><p>Shaw has been around the team plenty while in recovery mode, with a front-row seat to what’s been one of baseball’s best teams. The Cubs started Tuesday with a 35-16 record since June 11, the National League’s best mark and the sport’s second best in that span.</p><p>The Cubs started the season with championship-level aspirations that included Shaw playing a sizable role. While infielder <b>Pedro Ramirez</b> and outfielder <b>Michael Conforto</b> have kept the team’s bench productive without him, Shaw still figures to factor into a title chase, assuming the pain in his hand finally goes away.</p><p>“I see a really good team,” Shaw said. “We’ve known we’re going to be really good from the very beginning. We’ve gone through ups and downs … and here we are on the far end of it where we’re playing really well. … It’s really, really good baseball.</p><p>“You look at this team, and you’re like, ‘Wow, this is a really good team.’</p><p>“I’m pumped to get back out there and be helping any way I can. It’s been a great experience this year being around the boys. It’s obviously stunk a little bit being hurt, but it is what it is and we’ll be back and we’ll be rolling.”</p><h3><b>Shota smacked, Cubs win</b></h3><p>Lefty starter <b>Shota Imanaga</b> surrendered three homers in the Cubs’ 8-6 win over the Nationals on Tuesday.</p><p>When one of baseball’s most homer-prone pitchers meets baseball’s home-run leaders, that can happen.</p><p>Imanaga has allowed 28 long balls on the season, one shy of the major league lead. He’s been mostly fantastic this season, coming into Tuesday with a 2.06 ERA in his previous 10 starts, but home runs have remained an issue.</p><p>The Cubs’ bats backed their pitcher, matching the sport’s best offense with three homers of their own and lengthy at-bats that put pressure on Nationals pitching.</p><p>“I’m just thankful for them,” Imanaga said through an interpreter. “If I do give up runs, I believe that our offense is going to score them back.</p><p>“Today, I felt like if they didn’t score runs, I would have ruined the game. But having that belief that our offense is going to score runs, that allows me to be more aggressive.”</p><p></p><h3><b>Good and bad</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Righty pitchers <b>Edward Cabrera</b> and <b>Daniel Palencia</b> had minor league rehab outings with Double-A Knoxville on Tuesday.</p><p>While <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/07/cubs-edward-cabrera-starting-rotation-bullpen-playoffs-craig-counsell-tommy-hottovy-mlb-trade-deadline-jed-hoyer" >Cabrera</a> had a second consecutive solid showing, throwing five scoreless, hitless innings and striking out seven, Palencia struggled for a second straight rehab appearance, facing six batters, walking three of them and hitting another, tagged for four runs.</p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: Feds file new charges in botched Country Club Hills sting after initial case collapsed
entries.summary: <p>New charges have been filed over the June 9 attempted robbery<b> </b>of undercover federal officers in Country Club Hills, nearly two months after<b> </b>the case originally brought by prosecutors fell apart over video of a police shooting that seemed to contradict an FBI special agent’s sworn affidavit.</p><p>It’s one of a series of cases that prompted judges to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/18/boutros-holleb-hotaling-atf-country-club-hills" target="_blank" >question the feds’ credibility</a> in Chicago. U.S. Magistrate Judge Keri<b> </b>Holleb<b> </b>Hotaling, who handled the original case, at one point threatened to hold a hearing over whether to sanction the government over what had occurred.</p><p>That hearing never went forward.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/18/boutros-holleb-hotaling-atf-country-club-hills" >Charges dropped in suburban ATF sting, further straining trust between Boutros’ office and judges</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Now, new<b> </b>attempted robbery charges have been leveled against Amir<b> </b>Fagan, Darrion<b> </b>Rayford and<b> </b>Dontrell<b> </b>Gordon. Fagan is the only one of the three who also faced charges in June. He<b> </b>and Rayford<b> </b>were then charged<b> </b>June 30<b> </b>in a new indictment<b> </b>that was only unsealed Monday.</p><p>The feds charged Gordon separately<b> </b>in a criminal complaint<b> </b>filed Tuesday. Gordon<b> </b>had<b> </b>previously<b> </b>been misidentified<b> </b>as<b> </b>Demond<b> </b>Edwards, the man who was shot by a Chicago police officer during the Country Club Hills incident, according to a new FBI<b> </b>affidavit.</p><p>Edwards doesn’t face any known charges, and he<b> </b>is now suing<b> </b>the city of Chicago<b> </b>over his shooting. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/19/shooting-fbi-atf-hotaling-boutros-country-club-hills" target="_blank" >Video of the shooting</a><b> </b>prompted the collapse of the original case. And now, city lawyers<b> </b>say his lawsuit belongs in federal court partly because the officer had been under the supervision<b> </b>of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives.</p><p>The new criminal complaint<b> </b>filed against Gordon alleges<b> </b>Gordon, Fagan<b> </b>and<b> </b>Rayford<b> </b>tried<b> </b>to<b> </b>rob<b> </b>three people<b> </b>working undercover<b> </b>with<b> </b>the ATF<b> </b>at<b> </b>gunpoint<b> </b>during<b> </b>an<b> </b>$8,700<b> </b>gun transaction June 9<b> </b>on Loretto Lane in Country Club Hills.</p><p>Rayford and Gordon got away and were only arrested<b> </b>Monday.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" </b>Fagan, Edwards and<b> </b>Chashonn Toney. But the feds<b> </b>moved to dismiss<b> </b>the charges<b> </b>about a week later<b> </b>after video surfaced of the officer shooting Edwards.</p><p>The feds dropped the case without prejudice, meaning they could still file new charges.</p><p>U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros’ spokesman<b> </b>Joseph<b> </b>Fitzpatrick<b> </b>said Tuesday<b> </b>the case remains under investigation.</p><p>An FBI special agent swore in an affidavit in the original case that, according to the law enforcement officer who shot Edwards, “Edwards struck the law enforcement officer multiple times about his face and body with his fists.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/19/shooting-fbi-atf-hotaling-boutros-country-club-hills" >Video contradicts FBI agent’s account of shooting during undercover sting in Country Club Hills</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>No punches appear to be thrown<b> </b>in the video that surfaced. Prosecutors later argued that the video captured “approximately the last 25 seconds”<b> </b>of an encounter that lasted “for minutes,” and did not capture earlier interactions, “including Edwards striking”<b> </b>the officer.</p><p>The shooting is under investigation by Illinois State Police and the Civilian Office of Police Accountability.</p><p>The video also seemed to raise questions about whether people in the case had been properly identified. Frustrated by the apparent lack of due diligence by prosecutors,<b> </b>Holleb Hotaling said she’d hold a hearing<b> </b>to decide whether<b> </b>to sanction<b> </b>the feds.</p><p>She told attorneys June 18 that<b> </b>“this court is very concerned that I cannot rely on the information that is provided to me either from the U.S. attorney’s office or from agents … when I’m swearing out an affidavit now, right?”</p><p>Boutros’ office<b> </b>later argued<b> </b>the judge<b> </b>did not have the authority<b> </b>to hold such a hearing. She wound up agreeing to a “brief”<b> </b>delay<b> </b>but never rescheduled.</p>

entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams knows this is the time of year to fail — but time is running out
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback Caleb Williams figures now is the time to fail.</p><p></p><p>Time, though, is running short.</p><p></p><p>The Bears already have more <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/11/bears-training-camp-report-day-12-dandre-swift-shines-scrimmage-roschon-johnson-nfl" target="_blank" >training camp practices</a> in their rearview mirror than they have in front of them. The first preseason game looms Saturday — though it’d be surprising if starters play relevant snaps — with Week 1 four-and-a-half-weeks in the future.</p><p>There won’t be many more opportunities for Williams to do what he did Tuesday afternoon — face players in full pads chasing him. Williams was promising in the Bears’ scrimmage on the Halas Hall backfields, at one point covering 80 yards in two plays on throws to receivers Rome Odunze and Scotty Miller after being backed up on his 1-yard line.</p><p>He still needs to be more accurate — he led both Kalif Raymond and Colston Loveland too far on pass attempts earlier in practice — but appeared to break out of the stagnancy he showed during the second week of training camp.</p><p>For all the attention given him this offseason — “Madden 27,” the cover of which he graces, will be released Thursday — Williams still needs to grow considerably to get to where the Bears want him to be. That growth needs to happen on the backfields at Halas Hall. When the season begins, he’ll have fewer chances to make significant improvements in practice.</p><p>Williams started the first four-day chunk of training camp red-hot before plateauing over the past week. Tuesday, the Bears hope, was a turning point.</p><p>“That’s the point of this moment, this time, being able to go out there and fail,” Williams said. “Go out there and come back to the film room and correct it and go out there the next day … and correct it and get it right — so that Coach has the proper confidence in myself, but also the team to be able to go out there on game days.”</p><p>Coach Ben Johnson took the blame for some of Williams’ stagnancy before Tuesday’s practice. In two weeks, the Bears have installed, in Johnson’s estimation, 98% of their offense. The sheer volume of plays he installed was meant to test Williams — and for the coaching staff to better determine how to whittle down the Week 1 playbook.</p><p>“I've put in more this year on offense than I did a year ago by design …” Johnson said. “I want it to feel like a lot right now.”</p><p>Things started to slow down Tuesday. For the first time in camp, the Bears didn’t plan exactly what plays they were going to run in each drill. When the defense presented a certain coverage, Williams could change the play or the protection.</p><p>In the first two weeks, the Bears simply ran the plays that were called, making it harder to assess where certain players stood. Before practice, Johnson told Williams and the offense that Tuesday was “a big day of creating evidence.” It would weigh into “where everyone stands on the roster,” he said — and perhaps whether they’ll play against the Browns in Saturday’s exhibition debut. After meeting with general manager Ryan Poles on Wednesday, Johnson figures to have a playing-time game plan in place Thursday.</p><p>Part of what made Tuesday’s scrimmage so important for Williams was the possibility that he could play so little in preseason games. Rather, the Bears could rely on Tuesday’s scrimmage and joint practices with the Bengals and Titans the next two weeks to stress-test their quarterback.</p><p>Williams, for his part, said he didn’t have a preference for whether he’d play Saturday — or in the preseason at all. But he might have tipped his hand when he said he likes to treat practices and joint practices like games — “because that may be what I get, and that may not be what I get.”</p><p>Late in practice Tuesday, Williams was backed up on his own 1-yard line, needing two first downs to win the drill. After throwing the ball away on first down when rookie Dillon Thieneman blitzed from his blind side, Williams dropped back and considered checking the ball down to a running back. When a defensive end looked around in that direction, he fired to Odunze, whose catch-and-run up the right sideline went 58 yards.</p><p>On the next play, veteran Scotty Miller ran a crossing route. Williams lost sight of him for a second — “That's what happens when you're on the shorter end,” Williams said — before seeing him emerge between two linebackers. He caught the pass and slid down to end the drill.</p><p>Williams celebrated. It wasn’t a game, but it might have to do — at least until the Bears travel to Cincinnati for practice next week.</p><p>“He's taken complete control of what we're trying to do,” Johnson said. “And so we're on the right track.”</p><p>They’re not there yet.</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: No divine intervention for White Sox, who blow 4-run lead in loss to Reds
entries.summary: <p>All the pope hats in the world couldn’t save the White Sox in a 5-4, 10-inning loss to the Reds on Tuesday.</p><p>There was no divine intervention for an offense that had one hit in its last 19 at-bats. And perhaps other forces were at work in the game-turning eighth inning, when luck didn’t go the Sox’ way.</p><p>However it happened, the Sox let a 4-0 lead get away, disappointing a sellout crowd of 38,113 that came out for a pope hat in honor of Pope Leo, a lifelong Sox fan.</p><p>Sean Burke was brilliant, bouncing back from a rough start in Boston with seven innings of one-run ball. Only Eugenio Suarez gave him a problem, hitting a solo homer in the fifth. </p><p>"He was awesome," manager Will Venable said. "Feel like he one-ups himself every time he goes out there. Really good feel for the slider. Thought he got a ton of swing and miss on it. A good fastball again."</p><p>The Sox appeared to have the game in hand with solo homers by Brenton Doyle, Edgar Quero and Miguel Vargas and an RBI double by Sam Antonacci against Reds lefty Nick Lodolo.</p><p>In the eighth, Venable turned to left-handed reliever Bryan Hudson, who was the victim of rotten luck: an infield single, a bloop single just beyond second baseman Antonacci’s reach and a bouncing ball that found a hole for a run. Venable then turned to righty Grant Taylor, who allowed the game-tying two-run single to Tyler Stephenson.</p><p>“That’s baseball,” Venable said. “Just weren’t able to stop the bleeding.”</p><p>Meanwhile, the Sox were practically silent at the plate in the last six innings. Only Munetaka Murakami reached base, on a double in the eighth.</p><p>“Lodolo was tough. Obviously, we were able to put some really good swings on him,” Venable said. “And then we just couldn’t get anything cooking after that.”</p><p>The Reds took the lead on Elly de la Cruz’s sacrifice fly. The Sox went down meekly in the 10th.</p><p>“I’d trade a bad performance for a win,” Burke said. “A one-run game, the mistake to Suarez will eat at me a little bit. I shook off [Quero] and went with a fastball. He put a good swing on it.”</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" entries.title: Hanging on by a thread, safety-net hospitals brace for new blows
entries.summary: <p>Last month, two of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/26/3-people-fatally-shot-south-side" >six people</a> who were wounded in a mass shooting in Humboldt Park were treated at Mount Sinai Hospital. Mount Sinai was also one of eight Chicago Hospitals flagged in a recent <a class="Link" href="https://www.citizen.org/article/big-ugly-threat/" target="_blank" >report by Public Citizen</a> as being at high risk of closing under upcoming Medicaid cuts.</p><p>Writing in as a medical student and orthopedic trauma surgeon at the University of Chicago, we know from our own history that the city doesn't have to imagine the impacts of one of its major trauma centers closing. When U. of C. <a class="Link" href="https://chicagomaroon.com/20121/news/history-of-trauma-center-closing/" target="_blank" >closed its adult trauma center in 1988</a>, the South Side went nearly 30 years without one. People died on longer ambulance rides to hospitals up north. It took years of organizing by residents who had buried loved ones and neighbors to get a trauma center <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2018/5/8/18387887/u-of-c-trauma-center-sees-64-patients-in-first-week" >finally reopened in 2018</a>.</p><p>Our trauma center treats roughly 1,200 gunshot survivors a year, and <a class="Link" href="https://journals.lww.com/annalsofsurgery/abstract/9900/health_insurance_instability_following_firearm.1210.aspx" target="_blank" >nearly 1 in 3 of those survivors will lose their insurance within a year of their injury</a>. Without insurance to allow for follow-up care, minor complications become expensive emergency room visits that the hospital absorbs.</p><p>Safety-net hospitals have relied on <a class="Link" href="https://www.medicaid.gov/medicaid/financial-management/medicaid-disproportionate-share-hospital-dsh-payments" target="_blank" >Disproportionate Share Hospital payments</a> to offset these costs for decades. However, those payments are <a class="Link" href="https://www.aha.org/system/files/media/file/2020/02/fact-sheet-medicaid-dsh-0120.pdf" target="_blank" >set to be cut by roughly $24 billion</a>, but were <a class="Link" href="https://essentialhospitals.org/on-the-hill-house-passes-government-funding-package/" target="_blank" >delayed to 2028</a>. Medicaid already reimburses trauma care at rates <a class="Link" href="https://news.feinberg.northwestern.edu/2025/10/21/medicaid-billed-for-more-than-half-of-u-s-hospital-costs-from-gun-injuries/" target="_blank" >lower than the actual cost of treatment</a>, so with the rollbacks in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act projected to strip Medicaid coverage from millions of Americans, the unresolved future of the Disproportionate Share Hospital program does not leave these hospitals much room to balance their finances.</p><p>As 2028 approaches, we must remember it took far more to reopen the South Side's trauma center than it would have to keep it from closing. Rather than postponing these cuts again at the last minute, Congress should repeal them outright and help these hospitals continue to serve the communities most in need.</p><p><i>Armin Pazooki, medical student, University of Chicago Pritzker School of Medicine</i></p><p><i>Dr. Mary Kate Erdman, assistant professor of orthopedic surgery, University of Chicago</i></p><h3>Fix accessible crosswalk signals pronto</h3><p>Stand at a Chicago intersection and listen. If you can see the walk signal, you've probably never noticed there's anything to listen for. If you can't, that faint chirp or spoken word — when it exists at all — is the only thing standing between you and a six-lane crossing.</p><p>Last month, the federal monitor delivered its <a class="Link" href="https://dralegal.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/01_Plan_Year_1_Independent_Monitor_Annual_Report.pdf" target="_blank" >first report card</a> on Chicago's accessible crosswalk signals for impaired pedestrians. On paper it's a win: The city installed signals at <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/07/10/accessible-pedestrian-signals-court-monitor" target="_blank" >78 intersections</a>, eight more than required. Buried in the report is the number that matters more: Not one of the 103 inspected intersections was found fully compliant.</p><p>I've spent enough time around technical specifications to know what "not fully compliant" usually hides. It rarely means a broken device. More often, it's a locator tone mounted out of reach, a push button on the wrong pole, a vibrotactile arrow pointing a few degrees off or a spoken message that starts a beat late. </p><p>As Rachel Weisberg, an attorney at Disability Rights Advocates, told the Sun-Times, the signals are usable but not as effective as they should be. That's not acceptable.</p><p>Only 165 intersections have been installed so far. Fixing the process now is far cheaper than reopening thousands of intersections later. Chicago must install 110 more intersections this year, climbing to 245 by year eight. If every signal built today carries the same flaws, the city will reach 2040 having stacked thousands of devices without revisiting one. Fixing a foundation after the fact always costs more than pouring it right the first time.</p><p>An engineer's first instinct isn't to add more units — it's to check whether the process was "buttoned up" correctly from the start. Certify signals before they count. Test them with the people who use them. Measure compliance, not installation.</p><p>Chicago has 15 years left on this order. Let's get to work. For the person standing there, listening, the target shouldn't be a number that looks good on a news release. It should be one that lets them cross the street without guessing.</p><p><i>Yunus Tozal, civil engineer, Village of Niles</i></p><h3>In agreement about United Airline’s service </h3><p>It's most unfortunate that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/letters-to-the-editor/2026/08/08/weather-delay-flight-united-airlines-mental-health-black-teens-grocery-store-sox-pope-trump" >letter writer Bil Roby-Tubach </a>of Lincoln, Nebraska, had such a miserable experience with United Airlines employees at O'Hare Airport. It's a terrible reflection on our fair city. But it's not surprising. I spent decades flying in and out of O'Hare for business. Whenever possible, I avoided United and its loud, rude, arrogant employees on the ground and in the air. I found that all other airlines — U.S.-based and international carriers — were preferable.</p><p>I once dealt with a United flight attendant on a long flight from Europe who was so angry and over the top that I too filed a complaint. United's answer was a $500 voucher. Big deal.</p><p>United's newest TV commercial has the tag line: "You can take a lot of airlines out of Chicago. But you can never take the Chicago out of this airline." What does this even mean? I don't think it is a good reflection on Chicago, given United's lousy customer service reputation.</p><p>I'm sorry that Mr. Roby-Tubach might have gotten a poor impression of Chicago because of United employees. There are "friendly skies" up there. But not where United flies.</p><p><i>Blaise J. Arena, Des Plaines</i></p><h3>No question, Trump is a leader </h3><p>I take issue with reader Linda Hendelman's recent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/letters-to-the-editor/2026/08/10/japanese-americans-concentration-camps-immigrants-citizenship-department-natural-resources" target="_blank" >letter</a> saying Donald Trump can't be described as a "leader." She quotes Merriam-Webster's definition, “a capacity to lead,” and then inserts her own feelings. By claiming that Trump "pushed the country" proves she thinks he is a leader. Logic takes a back seat to her feelings. Trump Derangement Syndrome is alive and well.</p><p><i>Donald Nauyokas, Brighton Park</i></p><h3></h3>

entries.title: My wife is gone, but her push for colorectal cancer screenings lives on
entries.summary: <p>When I met Julie in 1996, I knew I had found the love of my life.</p><p>We were young, with more dreams than plans. But we believed that if we faced life together, everything else would fall into place. Before long, we were engaged, married and welcoming our first daughter, Baylee, into the world. Soon after came Mckenna and Jayden, completing the family Julie and I cherished more than anything.</p><p>Anyone who knew Julie knows she never did anything halfway. She poured her heart into everything she loved. As a former gymnast, she eventually turned her passion into purpose by opening I & M Gymnastics in Channahon, where she coached young athletes. But she taught far more than routines and competition skills. She taught work ethic, confidence, resilience, kindness and the value of lifting others up.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-cf0000" name="module-cf0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>Even after selling the gym to spend time with our family, Julie never stopped inspiring people. She immersed herself in bodybuilding and CrossFit, coached countless athletes, helped people improve their nutrition and encouraged all those in her orbit to become healthier versions of themselves.</p><p>Health wasn’t just something Julie believed in — it was how she lived. She was the epitome of health-conscious. That’s why her colorectal cancer diagnosis came as such a shock.</p><p>If someone as disciplined, active and committed to healthy living as Julie could face this disease, it became painfully clear to us that colorectal cancer doesn’t only affect people who appear unhealthy. It doesn’t always come with warning signs. And it doesn’t wait until life slows down.</p><p>Julie could have let her diagnosis define her. Instead, she chose to use it to educate others. She wanted people to understand that taking care of yourself means more than eating well and exercising. It also means keeping up with preventive health screenings that can detect disease before symptoms even appear.</p><p>Julie, who died in March 2024, hoped her experience would encourage someone else to schedule a screening he or she had been putting off. If sharing her story could spare another family from receiving the kind of news we did, she believed it was worth it.</p><p>There are still moments when Julie’s message reaches people. One of those moments came through a new <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/reel/DbVXkDQCc_3/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&igsh=MzRlODBiNWFlZA%3D%3D" target="_blank" >video </a>from the medicine company <a class="Link" href="https://guardanthealth.com/" target="_blank" >Guardant Health</a> honoring people who died from colorectal cancer and encouraging others to get screened. Seeing her name flashing on the screen was deeply emotional for our family. To see her name now tied to a message that could help someone get screened sooner felt like her mission was still moving forward.</p><p>Here in Illinois, an estimated<a class="Link" href="https://www.cancer.org/content/dam/cancer-org/research/cancer-facts-and-statistics/annual-cancer-facts-and-figures/2026/2026-cancer-facts-and-figures.pdf" target="_blank" > 6,160 people</a> will be diagnosed with colorectal — colon and rectal — cancer this year, and <a class="Link" href="https://www.cancer.org/content/dam/cancer-org/research/cancer-facts-and-statistics/annual-cancer-facts-and-figures/2026/2026-cancer-facts-and-figures.pdf" target="_blank" >2,080 are estimated to die </a>from the disease, according to the American Cancer Society. I can’t help but think that these numbers fall behind the harsh reality that many people become aware of having the disease too late.</p><p>When colorectal cancer is detected early, treatment is often more successful, and more lives are potentially saved. Too often, people assume they can wait. They feel healthy. They’re busy raising children, building careers or caring for everyone else before themselves.</p><p>Julie understood that feeling. But she also learned that feeling healthy isn’t always the same as being healthy.</p><p>Today, there are more screening options than ever before. Whether it’s a colonoscopy or another evidence-based screening option recommended by your healthcare provider, the most important step is making sure you get screened.</p><p>New options like <a class="Link" href="https://shieldcancerscreen.com/" target="_blank" >the Shield test,</a> the first U.S. Food and Drug Administration-approved blood test as a primary screening option for adults 45 and older who have an average risk of cancer, are quick and easy. All it takes is a conversation with your doctor, no special prep or procedure and no time away from work or life’s responsibilities.</p><p>In fact, the American Cancer Society recently <a class="Link" href="https://investors.guardanthealth.com/press-releases/press-releases/2026/American-Cancer-Society-Recommends-Guardant-Healths-Shield-Blood-Test-in-Updated-Colorectal-Cancer-Screening-Guidelines/default.aspx" target="_blank" >updated its colorectal cancer screening</a> guidelines to recommend Shield.</p><p>Talk to your loved ones, encourage your friends and, most importantly, don’t put off screening.</p><p>If reading this prompts just one person to schedule a colorectal cancer screening, then Julie’s greatest lesson will continue to save lives. That’s all she wanted.</p><p><i>Nicholas Tkaczuk is a licensed health insurance broker</i> <i>based in Channahon.</i> </p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-490000" name="module-490000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Daughter's Wedding Planning Has Been Hijacked
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My 33-year-old daughter is getting married, and the mothers have taken over her wedding plans. They want more than 200 guests, a full Catholic ceremony, fine wines, a full bar, plated dinner and a live band.</p><p>My daughter wants to please everyone but is not a practicing Catholic. She wants a small, intimate wedding with twinkling lights, a DJ and house wines from the California vineyard venue. Nothing she suggests is acceptable to the mothers, who see the ceremony as a means to impress their friends and business associates.</p><p>I divorced her mom years ago, but I'm still involved in my daughter's life. How can I advise her to take control of her wedding? — <i>DOTING DAD</i></p><p><b>DEAR DAD:</b> I tend to agree with you that a bride is entitled to the ceremony she wants, but sometimes there is no clear path to that end. No one will ever convince these moms to back off, and the repercussions of an elopement would be devastating.</p><p>My advice to the bride and groom is to grin and bear it. Let the mothers impress their friends (as long as they are willing to pay for it all), and the relaxation of the honeymoon will be all the sweeter.</p><p>Your daughter can save her more intimate plans for a renewal of vows ceremony held on a milestone anniversary. Obviously, she will want to avoid telling the moms about it until after all the arrangements are in place!</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> Our son, daughter-in-law and only grandchild live 1,400 miles away. We are able to see them only about three times a year. We have a warm, wonderful relationship. When we last visited, I noticed a picture in his room of our grandson, who is 1½ years old, with his babysitter. There are no pictures of us with him in the entire house. I would like our grandson to have pictures of us so he will remember us. Should I say anything? — <i>REALLY HURT IN CALIFORNIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR HURT:</b> Because you have a warm, wonderful relationship with your son and his family, the lack of photos of you with your grandson is likely not a deliberate slight. The next time you visit, ask them casually why there isn't one. Then ask one of them to snap some of the three of you and offer to have one framed for them.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My parents are retired. They live on a limited income and still support my 31-year-old brother, who lives rent-free in their basement. They told me how expensive their electric bill is becoming, and I asked why they don't have my brother help with expenses or pay rent? Abby, he makes close to $100,000 a year. They quickly changed the subject, and when I tried to circle back, I was told to drop it.</p><p>How can I help my parents see that what they are doing is hurting them, not helping their adult son? — <i>THEIR OTHER SON IN MAINE</i></p><p><b>DEAR SON:</b> There is truth to the adage, "You can lead a horse to water, but you can't make it drink." Understand that your parents must be deriving some satisfaction from encouraging your brother's dependency. Your attempt to help them resulted in their becoming defensive, so stop talking to them about it. HOWEVER, you should consider talking to your brother about the fact that the electric bills are now so steep it is causing your parents hardship and suggest he help out. It's worth a try.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p>

entries.title: Students spread the word to strapped Chicago renters about their shot at buying in the neighborhood
entries.summary: <p>Many Chicago renters have been <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/interactive/chicago-rents-climbing-fast-housing-crisis/" target="_blank" ><u>priced out</u></a> of apartments in their neighborhoods over the past few decades. In eight neighborhoods over the last year, however, a city ordinance gives tenants a shot at buying their building if it goes up for sale.</p><p>On the Northwest Side, where the <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/doh/supp_info/topa.html" target="_blank" ><u>Tenant Opportunity to Purchase Act</u></a> has been in effect for more than a year, city officials say only one tenant association has purchased their building, out of hundreds of property sales in the area. Seven tenant groups went through the process but were unable to buy the building, according to the city. One group of Logan Square renters has <a class="Link" href="https://blockclubchicago.org/2026/07/15/logan-square-renters-the-1st-to-sue-landlord-over-tenant-right-of-first-refusal-act-violation/" target="_blank" ><u>sued</u></a> their landlord for not complying with the ordinance. </p><p>The ordinance also went into effect in April around the Obama Presidential Center on the South Side. There have been no attempts to purchase in that area yet.</p><p>Many landlords and renters still don’t know about the ordinance, housing advocates say, and the process of buying a home is especially difficult for working-class renters.</p><p>Palenque LSNA, a nonprofit that has long pushed for affordable housing, is trying to change that — with help this summer from some young organizers.</p><p>On a sweltering recent day, dozens of students canvassed the changing Hermosa neighborhood on the Northwest Side. Their goal: getting the word out to renters how to potentially buy in their community.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure Palenque organizers are also campaigning for a city fund to help tenant associations with down payments.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-210000" name="image-210000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a833b5e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3970x2228+0+375/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc7%2F58%2Fbd26a44e4d3da632f08dc999a018%2Fimg-5381.jpeg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/607755d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3970x2228+0+375/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc7%2F58%2Fbd26a44e4d3da632f08dc999a018%2Fimg-5381.jpeg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ab19998/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3970x2228+0+375/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc7%2F58%2Fbd26a44e4d3da632f08dc999a018%2Fimg-5381.jpeg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Organizer Gary Jimenez prepares a group of students to canvas the Hermosa neighborhood on the Northwest Side with the group Palenque LSNA housing on July 21. About a decade ago, the landlord in the Humboldt Park apartment Jimenez’ family lived in announced a rent hike in order to make some repairs to the building. Jimenez’ parents — a truck driver and a factory worker — couldn’t afford the new amount, and the family had to move out. They bounced around from place to place until his mom could buy a home several blocks west. "I was gentrified out of my neighborhood,” he said. “I’m really passionate about ensuring [that] people that look like me continue living in the neighborhood that they grew up in.”</p>

entries.title: Bohemian National Cemetery concerts will take place despite investigation
entries.summary: <p>A series of music concerts scheduled at Bohemian National Cemetery in August and September will go on as planned, in spite of a new investigation into the North Park property over the alleged mishandling of human remains.</p><p>As <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/09/bohemian-national-cemetery-under-investigation-for-improperly-stored-remains-equipment-failures" target="_blank" ><u>reported</u></a> by the Sun-Times on Sunday, Illinois Comptroller Susana A. Mendoza announced that her office is inspecting procedures at the cemetery after a tip uncovered “multiple equipment failures and some human remains waiting to be cremated,” according to a statement. The remains have since been cremated and delivered to families.</p><p>The Bohemian National report comes on the heels of a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/06/decomposing-bodies-found-funeral-home-south-chicago-chapel-95th-street" target="_blank" ><u>separate investigation</u></a> into the South Chicago Chapel funeral home in South Deering after the mishandled remains of more than 50 deceased individuals were uncovered on Aug. 6.</p><p>Bohemian National Cemetery, a sprawling property with historic ties, has been an occasional, if eclectic, site for music for more than a decade. Empty Bottle Presents has staged the Beyond the Gate series at Bohemian National Cemetery since 2013, bringing a range of performers from Kim Gordon to Godspeed You! Black Emperor and William Basinski over the years.</p><p>Similar events happen at cemeteries around the country, most notably Los Angeles’ Hollywood Forever Cemetery and have become a popular draw for music fans.</p><p>While the investigation into Bohemian National Cemetery remains ongoing, organizers with Empty Bottle Presents told WBEZ/Sun-Times that a previously planned slate of concerts on the grounds will move forward.</p><p>“The Beyond the Gate events in [September] are still on as planned,” said Brent Heyl, director of music at parent company 16” on Center about the upcoming concerts. The fall calendar features Welsh baroque pop artist Cate Le Bon with local indie rock band Horsegirl on Sept. 25, followed by a pair of local instrumental metal acts, Russian Circles and Pelican, on Sept. 26.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-840000" name="image-840000"></a> <picture previously planned slate of concerts on the grounds will move forward.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Taylor Glascock for WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>An earlier show scheduled for Aug. 29 also remains on the schedule. The memorial gathering and concert to honor late guitarist Bo Lueders of Chicago hardcore act Harms Way who passed away in April was planned as a separate event to benefit the Night Ministry, Chicago Recovery Alliance and Hope For The Day.</p><p>“We understand the cemetery has addressed all concerns with the city and is on a path to be in good standing,” Heyl said. “We are in close contact to ensure that in the case. We have cherished over 10 years of shows together celebrating life, music and community.”</p><p>Requests for comment from representatives with Bohemian National Cemetery and Mendoza’s office were not answered as of press time. While entertainment behemoth Live Nation lists the Cate Le Bon show date on its website, a representative responded that “Empty Bottle shows aren't promoted by Live Nation.”</p><p>Alderman Samantha Nugent (39th Ward) referred requests about special event permits to the Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events (DCASE) who did not respond to inquiries. Alderwoman Nugent called the reports coming out of Bohemian National Cemetery “deeply troubling” in a statement.</p><p>“Every person deserves to be treated with dignity and respect in death, and every family deserves the peace of knowing their loved one has been properly laid to rest,” the statement read. “My office is closely monitoring the investigation and will remain in contact with the appropriate officials to ensure these issues are addressed.”</p><p>Empty Bottle’s Beyond the Gate Series began more than a decade ago with local experimental artist Wrekmeister Harmonies, who wanted a unique environment to perform his 2013 album, “You’ve Always Meant So Much to Me.” He was granted access to the North Side graveyard, established in 1877 by Czech immigrants as a non-denominational final resting place.</p><p>Today, Bohemian National Cemetery is on the National Registry of Historic Places. Up to 1,500 tickets can be available for the concerts there, which are set up on a lawn in between the wings of a mausoleum, away from grave plots.</p><p>As general manager Elizabeth Raleigh <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/music/2024/06/05/bohemian-national-cemetery-concert-kim-gordon-sonic-youth" target="_blank" ><u>previously told WBEZ</u></a> in 2024 ahead of a show featuring noise rock pioneer Kim Gordon, the concert series gives a wider perspective of what the cemetery stands for and the proceeds help offset rising maintenance costs.</p><p>“It shows we appeal to different cultures. It shows we’re open to everything, I mean, every culture, every nationality,” said Raleigh. “So we have a lot of different people coming, you know, people that like string quartets, people who like rock and roll. So it’s really a diverse thing.”</p>

entries.title: It’s last call for Wishbone. Regulars will remember ‘comfort’
entries.summary: <p>A couple years after Joel and Julie Nickson opened the Southern-inflected Wishbone restaurant at 1800 W. Grand Ave. in 1990, Bill Grant came in for the first time on a friend’s suggestion and ordered the Cajun-style shrimp with cheesy grits.</p><p>He’s been ordering them for breakfast ever since, usually twice a month.</p><p>“I’ve had shrimp and grits at 100 places across America, and these are still the absolute best to me,” said Grant.</p><div class="Enhancement FormEnhancement" data-align-center> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Crunchy French toast and shrimp and grits with cornbread are staples at Wishbone.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The Nicksons opened their restaurant 36 years ago in July on a shoestring budget. Over the years, they added dinner and lunch and expanded to Roscoe Village and Berwyn (both since closed). They moved locations a handful of times — notably to 1001 W. Washington Blvd., near Oprah Winfrey’s Harpo Studios, where it operated for 26 years and became a linchpin in a neighborhood going from gritty to gourmet. Then it moved to its current location at 161 N. Jefferson St., which the Nicksons have leased since 2018.</p><p>The constant throughout has been customers and staff, many of whom have tenures here exceeding two decades. Even now that the West Loop has become a dining destination, there’s no place quite like this one, they say.</p><p>“It’s like there’s going to be a hole,” said Ken Koehn, who has been coming to Wishbone since he moved to the West Loop in 2003. “The minute I moved into the neighborhood, it’s always been here. It's going to feel very strange.”</p><p>Koehn playfully credits his godmother with persuading him to buy his condo once she glimpsed the Wishbone sign from the balcony. He soon became a regular after work.</p><p>“I didn’t feel like cooking dinner, so I’d walk the three extra blocks and sit at the counter. After a while, you get to know all the staff. Joel was always there, and he’d always send out dessert for me. If they had split pea soup, the manager would text me that day and let me know. It just became such a welcoming place, like a family.”</p><p>That morning, he was in with a couple of co-workers for another favorite: the cornflake-coated crunchy French toast drizzled with maple syrup.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-480000" name="image-480000"></a> <picture </div><p>Wishbone has endured a lot of changes since the early days when the beat cops called it a “yuppie place” and Joel couldn’t give the shrimp and grits away. When it moved to Washington, it benefited from “the Oprah factor,” drawing celebrities and athletes alike thanks to the TV star’s frequent endorsements and its proximity to her studio.</p><p>“Oprah was a godsend,” Joel recalled. “Everybody thought she owned [Wishbone]. We’d get all the guests and celebrities coming in. We had a lot of good times.”</p><p>There was fame of the salacious ilk as well, as Wishbone was uncovered among the restaurants where city officials purportedly accepted bribes in the 1990s. The restaurant’s name became part of a corruption scandal uncovered in the dramatic FBI probe known as <a class="Link" href="https://news.wttw.com/2018/11/19/new-podcast-city-digs-dirt-old-chicago-scandal" target="_blank" ><u>Operation Silver Shovel</u></a>.</p><p>“I think the line was, ‘At Wishbone nobody noticed a bad suit, and it was noisy,’” Joel recalled of the coverage. “We definitely had a variety here, the cops and the robbers.”</p><p>They mostly came for the comforting, scratch-made food — red eggs soused in ancho chile sauce with black beans and corn tortillas; blackened catfish, collard greens cooked down with smoked turkey wings; and gently sweet, corn-studded muffins made by 30-year kitchen vet Oswaldo. They’d take it to go or stay and eat beneath the bright, surrealist paintings of chickens and barnyard scenes by Lia Nickson, Joel’s mother.</p><p>“Just this week I said I’m gonna get something different, and I still never have,” said Adrienne Banks, a regular who works at the Chicago Transit Authority next door. She, along with co-workers Nancy Sanchez and Tresa Mann had stopped by for their usual two-eggs breakfast special, which they order for carryout at least once a week. “We were sad to hear it was closing, so we’re just going to keep coming,” Banks added.</p><p>“It’s where we eat; It’s the <i>only</i> place we eat!” added Sanchez. “It’s affordable; you get more than what you pay for. It’s not just a meal. It’s the customer service, the smiles, looking forward to seeing people we know. They make you feel like family.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-7c0000" name="image-7c0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9698d9e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd0%2F33%2F4b1169e34277871ec5c1c959e341%2Fwishbonerequiem-260812-18.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8595445/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd0%2F33%2F4b1169e34277871ec5c1c959e341%2Fwishbonerequiem-260812-18.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6ac889b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd0%2F33%2F4b1169e34277871ec5c1c959e341%2Fwishbonerequiem-260812-18.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Customers eat at Wishbone in the West Loop, Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026.
