Since COVID, breakfast and lunch never fully recovered. It doesn’t help that competitors now crowd the streets around Wishbone, a far cry from the early days.</p><p>“Fridays used to be our busiest day; now they’re our slowest,” Joel said.</p><p>The Nicksons first talked about closing the restaurant about a year ago, when they stopped serving dinner but hung on mainly for the staff. The week before posting the announcement on social media, Joel gathered the 30-plus staff together and told them.</p><p>“That was the hard part,” Joel said. Now, the Nicksons are focused on getting as many as possible placed in new jobs. A handful have already taken positions at Sweet Maple Cafe on Taylor Street.</p><p>“It’s so sad!” said Omar Alonso, a server who’s worked at Wishbone for 25 years. “It really is like a family.”</p><p>“A dysfunctional family,” Joel piped up.</p><p>“They all like that, you know?” laughed fellow server Rigo Roberto, who started at Wishbone 26 years ago. “We’ve had our moments.”</p><p>Joel, meanwhile, mentioned for the second time that he was behind on his buttermilk pies. They’re Lia’s recipe, though he likes to sub in graham cracker crust. Yet every time he’d make his way back toward the kitchen, another customer would call his name from their table or wrap him into a hug.</p><p>“How are you? I can’t believe it!” one said, tearing up as he embraced Nickson.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a entries.title: Lights out for a Roscoe Village cafe's outdoor dining — even as others shine on
entries.summary: <p>Mitch Einhorn, co-owner of Lush Wine & Spirits, was floored this spring when a city inspector showed up at his Roscoe Village cafe and told him to take down the strings of decorative white lights around his outdoor seating area.</p><p>The lights weren't any different from those adorning close to a dozen other outdoor dining areas nearby.</p><p>But the inspector from the Department of Business Affairs and Consumer Protection said decorative lights aren't allowed in the public way, which is where sidewalk cafes sit.</p><p>Who knew? </p><p>Certainly not Einhorn.</p><p>The Chicago Sun-Times reviewed about 12 blocks across three North Side neighborhoods and found more than 40 restaurants, bars and other businesses had string lights decorating their sidewalk dining areas.</p><p>They light up outdoor dining areas on Lincoln Avenue in North Center and Lincoln Square; on Randolph and<b> </b>West Fulton Market streets, west of Halsted Street; and on Roscoe Street in Roscoe Village, within a few blocks of Einhorn's business.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a In some instances, the cords are hidden inside a conduit mounted on a pergola.</p><p>Elisa Sledzinska, BACP's deputy commissioner for communications and outreach, says the glowing lights are "not legal." </p><p>"Under the Municipal Code of Chicago, string lights are not permitted in sidewalk cafes," she said in an email. </p><p>It's unclear if the lights aren't allowed because of safety or other concerns.</p><p>She said the agency "conducts complaint-driven investigations at businesses throughout the City of Chicago to ensure compliance with Chicago's Municipal Code," and those usually originate with calls to 311. </p><p>Einhorn says he doesn't know who filed the complaint that prompted the inspector's visit to Lush.</p><p>But he's ticked off that the inspector didn’t walk Roscoe Street to see the dozen or so businesses with similar white lights.</p><p>"This is an issue in every ward. This comes down to uneven enforcement," he says. he could apply for a special use permit for the lights but was told there's no way to apply because no such permit exists.</p><p>Einhorn said Ald. Scott Waguespack's staffer told his brother and business partner, Cliff, that they'd look into the issue. Waguespack's 32nd Ward includes Roscoe Village's many sidewalk dining spots on its namesake street.</p><p>Waguespack's office didn't respond to requests for comment. </p><p>Ald. Walter Burnett (27th), whose ward includes lively outdoor dining areas in Fulton Market, didn't respond to a request for comment.</p><p>An Illinois Restaurant Association spokeswoman said, "We are going to pass on this opportunity [to comment]."</p><p>For other sidewalk cafe operators, there doesn't appear to be any terrible consequences for breaking the no-lights rule.</p><p>Einhorn wasn't fined; he was simply told to take down his lights.</p><p>This means most business owners would probably say: Let there be light.</p><p>Einhorn says he would, too — if he could.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/small-business/2026/02/07/lush-wine-spirits-roscoe-village-einhorn-tariffs" >Happy times at Lush Wine & Spirits, if not for tariff uncertainty</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/09/22/chicago-restaurants-dog-ban-lift-timmy-knudsen-lincoln-park-council-member" >City Council member proposes lifting Chicago’s ban on dogs in restaurants</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Shipwrecks, mussels and sponges: Chicago has scuba diving history
entries.summary: <p>On a cloudy, 80-degree summer day, I squeezed myself into a full-length rubber wetsuit, pulled a tight hood over my head and shimmied my hands into some thick gloves. Several miles away in Lake Michigan from our starting point in Hammond, Indiana, my fellow scuba divers sweated it out on the boat while waiting to plunge into the water.</p><p>In Chicago, the 109-foot Silver Spray is the only shipwreck you can spot from DuSable Lake Shore Drive. The ship ran aground in 1914 at the Morgan Shoals, an ancient reef where many ships have met their end.</p><p>An estimated 6,000-10,000 shipwrecks are at the bottom of the Great Lakes, but the largest share lies in Lake Michigan. To see those, you’ll need to get in the water.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-c50000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Double Action Dive Charters takes scuba divers out in Lake Michigan to visit some sunken barges on July 25, 2026.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Susie An/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“These are archaeological sites that tell us part of the vital history of Chicago’s development,” said Madeline Crispell, curator at the Chicago Maritime Museum.</p><p>I recently visited a couple of these so-called archaeological sites. For some, Lake Michigan is a beloved scuba diving destination, specifically because of the shipwrecks, well preserved by the cold, fresh water. While Chicago has a small but robust scuba scene, there’s an even deeper history to this form of diving that goes beyond the wrecks. The world’s largest scuba certification organization traces its roots back to the Chicago suburbs. It turns out, going diving in the Great Lakes prepares you for a lot.</p><h3><b>Chicago’s connection to scuba</b></h3><p>In the early 1950s, Chicago Park District purchased a pair of Aqua-Lungs, co-invented by Jacques Cousteau about a decade earlier. It was the earliest form of scuba gear. The waters of Lake Michigan were dangerous, and the equipment was meant to assist lifeguards in search-and-rescue operations.</p><p>One of the first Chicago lifeguards to try out the Aqua-Lung was Ralph Erickson, a swim instructor at the Northwest Side Portage Park pool. His daughter Karina Erickson said he was given no instruction or training.</p><p>“He got in the pool and started swimming with this brand new piece of technology,” she said. “He found that he was now able to be fully neutrally buoyant and didn’t need to come up for air. He thought it was the most incredible thing.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-7c0000" name="image-7c0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Ralph Erickson exits the water after going scuba diving.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Karina Erickson</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>In the early days, most people became scuba divers for professional reasons, because they were lifeguards, in the Navy or salvaging shipwrecks. But by the 1960s, people started considering scuba just for fun.</p><p>Erickson wanted to introduce people to scuba in a safe way. So he wrote one of the first instructional manuals and used it to teach scuba courses in Chicago.</p><p>He linked up with another Chicagoan, John Cronin, who sold scuba equipment. The two decided to form a dive instruction organization.</p><p>Within a few months, Cronin turned his basement in Niles into the headquarters for what would later become the world’s largest scuba organization. In 1966, they launched the Professional Association of Diving Instructors (PADI), which has certified more than 30 million divers in 186 countries.</p><p>Erickson certified a few of those divers himself, including Marianne Preker, owner of the Lakeview neighborhood dive shop Underwater Safaris.</p><p>“I think what Ralph and John did is take something and make it available to common, ordinary people to have fun,” Preker said. “PADI was the first organization to have a certification card with your picture on it. That made the whole thing safer.”</p><h3><b>Diving in Lake Michigan</b></h3><p>Most Midwesterners think of scuba as something done on vacation, perhaps in the warm waters of the Caribbean or off the coast of Florida where you can see coral reefs and colorful fish.</p><p>But it turns out Chicago has its own scuba scene. Katie Mika is one of the founders of Chicago Undersea Explorers Society (CUES), a local scuba club with roughly fifty active members. “Half the fun is diving with your friends,” Mika said.</p><p>CUES goes on several local dives each summer. I joined them for a wreck dive of two sunken barges off the coast of Hammond, Indiana in July.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure I finally jumped in the water with great relief after sweating in the heat. Though I’ve been a certified diver for decades, this was my first time diving in the Great Lakes. The most notable difference was the visibility. In the Caribbean, the best visibility for diving can reach beyond 100 feet. Fellow founding member of the Chicago Undersea Explorers Society, Andria Kessler, said the standards are quite different in Lake Michigan. “A very good visibility day is 15-20 feet, but weather changes and sometimes it’s 5 feet.”</p><p>We had poor visibility on our dives, and that can be disorienting, especially for newer divers. Yet despite only being able to see about 5 feet, it was clear that these wrecks have become artificial reefs, supporting a whole ecosystem. I found invasive zebra and quagga mussels covering the wrecks. In addition to seeing a few fish, I also found living sponges the size of a half-dollar coin on our second wreck of the day, the Material Service barge. The barge sank during a violent storm in 1936. 15 crew members lost their lives.</p><p>Mika is a marine biologist and said scuba diving gives you a real appreciation for the lake’s ecosystem. “I think class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Alexandra Usher</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div>Alexandra Usher works at the University of Chicago and lives in the Bucktown neighborhood with her husband and two children. Over the years, she’s spent a lot of time driving back and forth on DuSable Lake Shore Drive to Hyde Park. On high-traffic days, she had time to stare off in the water, and she noticed the remnants of a wreck poking up just off the shore at 49th Street in the Kenwood neighborhood.<br><br>“It just looks like something strange sticking out of the water,” she said. “You can see the waves breaking on it. And no, it’s not clear that it’s a shipwreck.”<br><br>The 109-foot Silver Spray was on its way to pick up 200 University of Chicago students for a tour of the Gary, Indiana, steel mills in 1914. It got a little too close to the Morgan Shoals, an ancient reef where many ships have run aground.<br><br>“It’s one of the more amusing anecdotes of a shipwreck in the Chicago area,” said Madeline Crispell, curator at the Chicago Maritime Museum.<br><br>Only the captain and six crew members were on board and they were so close to shore they weren’t in any real danger. Crispell said they allegedly took their time evacuating because they wanted to eat the Irish stew the chef had made for lunch.</div> </div><p></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-750000" name="html-embed-module-750000"></a><script async src="https://modules.wearehearken.com/wbez/embed/4190.js"></script> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: More severe storms, damaging winds may hit south suburbs; over 142,000 still without power in Chicago area
entries.summary: <p>After the south suburbs were rocked by at least three tornadoes Tuesday, additional severe weather could hit the area as over 142,000 ComEd customers remain without power Wednesday morning. </p><p>A severe thunderstorm watch was in effect for Joliet, Kankakee, DeKalb until 1 p.m., according to the National Weather Service. Severe weather could bring downpours and gusty winds, though the storms may not be as strong as Tuesday's severe weather. </p><p>"Most areas are not gonna see severe winds, but if you do, you could see winds as high as 70 miles per hour," Gino Izzi, a meteorologist with the weather service said. </p><p>A line of thunderstorms was expected to move through the Chicago area late Wednesday morning and between a quarter and half of an inch of rain was possible closer to the city, according to the weather service.</p><p>Over 142,000 ComEd customers remained without power Wednesday morning after Tuesday's severe weather, according to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.comed.com/outages/experiencing-an-outage/outage-map" target="_blank" >ComEd outage map</a>. </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/11/severe-weather-expected-in-chicago-area-and-other-areas-of-illinois" target="_blank" >Three tornadoes with gusts of 86 to 110 mph</a> were confirmed Tuesday: One in southern Cook County, another in eastern Will County, and the third in the Mokena area, also in Will County.</p><p>Rick Johnson, a Mokena resident of more than 30 years, said his home lost power — the same as it did last month for four days during another round of storms. He said he’s never experienced so many powerful and destructive storms in a single summer.</p><p>“It’s been an odd year,” he said.<br></p>

entries.title: Will East St. Louis transfer QB Jadon Wilson blossom into a star for No. 7 St. Francis?
entries.summary: <p>St. Francis has reloaded for its <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2025/12/02/providence-catholic-football-state-championship-ihsa-st-francis" >Class 5A state title</a> defense. The preseason No. 7 Spartans picked up seven transfers over the summer, including Jadon Wilson, a possible star quarterback.</p><p>The 6-3, 190-pound junior was the backup quarterback at East St. Louis last season and is bursting with confidence.</p><p>“I can make every play on the field,” Wilson said. “If you want me to run the ball, I can run it. If you need me to throw the ball 60 yards, I can throw it. If you need me to throw it short, I can throw it.”</p><p>Spartans coach Bob McMillen says that “all arrows are pointing to [Wilson] being the starter Week 1.”</p><p>“He believes he may have been overlooked at East St. Louis and wants to show everyone his talents,” McMillen said. “He has a little chip on his shoulder. A nice little edge. He’s extremely smart, unbelievably athletic and has a cannon for an arm.”</p><p>Junior Blake Lohman returns at receiver for St. Francis and is joined by three transfers. Junior receivers Greg Bess-Henning and Noah Turner joined from Carmel and Alijah Valeri, who started high school at St. Francis, is back after a year in Wisconsin.</p><p>“The receiver group is spectacular,” Wilson said. “Wherever I throw it, they go get it. We are going to do special things.”</p><p>Senior running back Tivias Caldwell Jr. rushed for nine TDs and more than 900 yards last season.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydlrhhky-l-o/" target="_blank" >Stephanie Zimmermann</a></h5><p><b>Delay and profit</b>: A new analysis shows that delaying home insurance claims for just a day or a week can add millions of dollars in profit collectively for the insurance industry.</p><p><b>The analysis</b>: For each day of delays on home insurance claims, the industry takes in an extra $8.8 million in interest and investment income, according to an analysis by the independent financial institution rating firm Weiss Ratings for the nonprofit Consumer Federation of America, which looked at the money that home insurers take in as premiums as well as their investment income. </p><p><b>All insurance</b>: Across all lines of property and casualty insurance — including home, auto, business and other coverage — the industry gains a combined $52.3 million in investment income for each additional day claims are delayed, the analysis found.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydlrhhky-l-il/" target="_blank" >Elijah James</a></h5><p>Amid the humid mist and roaring waterfalls inside Brookfield Zoo’s Tropic World habitat, a new, tiny resident clung tightly to its mother last week as a Sun-Times reporter visited.</p><p>A newborn squirrel monkey was born July 30 to mother Gizmo and father Sandy. While the infant does not yet have a name and its sex remains unidentified, it is already thriving, spending its first days riding securely on its mother’s chest and back as she navigates the habitat.</p><p>Guests will have a chance to see the newborn squirrel monkey and the rest of the primates inside the Tropic World exhibit daily during regular park hours.</p><p>The newborn enters an active group of six squirrel monkeys, including aunts and older sibling Slim, who was born in a previous litter and is learning maternal behaviors by watching Gizmo. For now, the newborn will remain dependent on mom.</p><p>"It'll be a while before they actually go off on their own," said Kim Skelton, director of primate care and conservation at Brookfield Zoo Chicago, of the newborn.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydlrhhky-l-ir/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>How has this summer's slate of intense storms affected your community?</b></p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Reply to this question via email</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). entries.title: Aspira se declara en bancarrota y podría quedarse con la venta de edificio financiado con dinero público
entries.summary: <p>En un tramo concurrido al norte de Milwaukee Avenue, las ventanas de cuatro pisos de un elegante edificio de piedra caliza blanca reflejan la falta de actividad a pocas semanas del inicio de clases.</p><p>El estado gastó $27 millones para construir la que fuera una escuela chárter hace poco más de una década. Pero en lugar de prepararse para recibir a los estudiantes, el edificio en Avondale está a punto de ser vendido a una empresa de inversión inmobiliaria por una fracción de lo que los contribuyentes pagaron para construirlo.</p><p>El antiguo operador de la escuela chárter, Aspira Inc. de Illinois, presentó recientemente una solicitud de bancarrota, luego de verse obligado a cerrar dos escuelas en marzo, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/02/27/mas-de-500-estudiantes-se-veran-desplazados-por-el-cierre-de-las-secundarias-charter-aspira" target="_blank" >lo que obligó a más de 500 estudiantes a transferirse a mitad de año</a>. En documentos presentados en la corte de bancarrota, la organización sin fines de lucro citó la pérdida de financiamiento por parte de las Escuelas Públicas de Chicago (CPS) y un “grave y continuo estrés financiero”.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c90000" name="module-c90000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>La situación plantea preguntas sobre si Aspira podrá embolsarse dinero de la venta de su edificio financiado con fondos públicos para cubrir sus propias operaciones. También no está claro si CPS o el estado podrán recuperar algo de la venta después de haber enviado millones a Aspira.</p><p>En documentos judiciales, los funcionarios de Aspira han indicado que quieren vender el edificio de Milwaukee Avenue y usar el dinero para saldar deudas y mantener operaciones en alguna medida.</p><p>La directora ejecutiva interina, Melissa Batista, señaló que Aspira todavía opera una escuela secundaria alternativa pública dentro de CPS que reingresa a alumnos que habían abandonado y que dirige programas de desarrollo juvenil y de participación comunitaria en el Aspira Community Center.</p><p>“De cara al futuro, nuestro enfoque está en reconstruir y renovar a ASPIRA mientras volvemos a las raíces de la organización centradas en la educación, el liderazgo juvenil y el servicio a nuestras comunidades”, escribió en un comunicado el martes. “Hay desafíos significativos por delante, pero también existe la oportunidad de reconstruir con intención”.</p><p>Cuando el estado le dio a Aspira dinero para construir su edificio en Milwaukee Avenue, los funcionarios elogiaron el compromiso de la organización comunitaria “con la autodeterminación de los jóvenes latinos y otros jóvenes desatendidos”.</p><p>Ahora, Iris Martínez, la exsenadora estatal demócrata que ayudó a Aspira a obtener las subvenciones de Springfield, dijo que la situación es “un desastre en todos los sentidos”. Martinez culpó a los administradores y a los miembros de la junta de Aspira, pero señaló que no ve manera de que el estado recupere su inversión.</p><p>“Ver que hoy la escuela está allí vacía, con la posibilidad de que una inmobiliaria la compre y probablemente la convierta en condominios, eso me rompe el corazón”, dijo Martínez.</p><p>Un portavoz del Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity, que otorgó las subvenciones a Aspira, afirmó el martes que funcionarios de la agencia están investigando el asunto tras las preguntas de WBEZ.</p><p>Mientras tanto, el contrato de Aspira con CPS, como todos los contratos chárter del distrito, especifica que si Aspira deja de operar sus escuelas, la organización “deberá” devolver “cualquier propiedad o activo” usado para operar sus escuelas que se haya comprado con dinero de CPS. La ley estatal busca aclarar cualquier ambigüedad al decir que todo aquello “comprado con fondos públicos deberá ser devuelto al distrito escolar” del cual la chárter obtuvo sus inscripciones.</p><p>En la última década, CPS envió $156 millones a Aspira para operar sus escuelas chárter, incluyendo $8 millones en estipendios por instalaciones para el edificio de Milwaukee Avenue.</p><p>En el pasado, algunos han dicho que CPS no trabajó lo suficiente para recuperar activos de las chárters cerradas. Jen Conant, la presidenta de la división chárter del Chicago Teachers Union, dijo que esta vez debe ser diferente, especialmente porque CPS le daba a Aspira dinero adicional cada año para operar en instalaciones fuera de CPS.</p><p>“Si CPS no recupera los fondos adicionales de la venta del edificio de Milwaukee, otros operadores chárter aprenderán que pueden abrir una escuela y aprovechar fondos públicos para hacerlo, cerrarla en pocos años y marcharse con los bienes raíces y el capital financiados por los contribuyentes para sus propios fines privados”, dijo. “Los fondos públicos, el dinero de las escuelas públicas, son para la educación de nuestros niños, no para que operadores privados jueguen con ellos”.</p><p>Los funcionarios de Aspira no respondieron preguntas sobre lo que creen que CPS tiene derecho a recibir.</p><h3>Los edificios de Aspira valen millones, pero ¿a dónde irá ese dinero?</h3><p>Los activos más importantes de Aspira son dos edificios en Avondale que albergaban escuelas secundarias, según muestran los registros de la corte, el moderno en Milwaukee Avenue y otro edificio más antiguo a menos de una milla al oeste de Barry Avenue que Aspira compró y renovó.</p><p>Los documentos de la corte revelan que las dos propiedades están vinculadas. La propiedad de Barry Avenue fue tasada en $4.5 millones, mucho menos de lo que los funcionarios de Aspira creían que valía. En una resolución de abril, los miembros de la junta citaron ese menor valor estimado como una de las razones por las que aprobaron presentar la bancarrota.</p><p>Aspira todavía debe $5.4 millones en una hipoteca sobre la propiedad de Barry Avenue, muestran los registros de la corte, y la organización pretende usar los ingresos de la venta de Milwaukee Avenue para pagar esa hipoteca.</p><p>Cuando Aspira puso a la venta el edificio de Milwaukee Avenue, <a class="Link" href="https://images1.showcase.com/d2/RutaJhL163YxVze3jesqELgIqTH9LQRuJ30-mKM00F4/document.pdf" target="_blank" >el anuncio inmobiliario resaltaba</a> que se mantiene en estado impecable y que ha recibido “una inversión de capital significativa” que “apoyaría su uso continuado o una reutilización adaptativa sin problemas”.</p><p>El anuncio también indica que el edificio cuenta con “certificación LEED Gold”, lo que significa que cumple altos estándares ambientales y de eficiencia energética.</p><p>No tardó mucho en que Aspira encontrara comprador. La semana pasada, Aspira informó a la corte de bancarrota que la organización había aceptado una oferta de $11 millones de Saxony Properties, LLC, un millón menos de lo que Aspira esperaba obtener. Aspira comparecerá ante la corte el 25 de agosto para intentar obtener la aprobación de la venta.</p><p>El propietario de Saxony Properties, que posee y alquila docenas de apartamentos en el norte, no respondió a una llamada ni a un correo electrónico preguntando qué planea hacer con el edificio.</p><p>En documentos de la corte, Aspira afirma que $11 millones es un precio “justo y razonable” y declara que Saxony no es una parte interesada y que el contrato se negoció a “distancia de mercado”.</p><p>Aspira indicó en documentos de la corte que usaría las ganancias de la venta del edificio de Milwaukee Avenue “para liquidar las deudas de los acreedores y financiar las operaciones del deudor o el plan de reorganización”.</p><p>Si se le permite a Aspira vender el edificio, la primera deuda que debe saldar es los $5.4 millones que le debe a Old Second National Bank, que tiene la hipoteca sobre la propiedad de Barry Avenue. A continuación recibirá pago el abogado inmobiliario, un expresidente de la junta de Aspira, que obtendrá $27,500.</p><p>Aspira proporcionó a la corte una larga lista de otras deudas que necesitan ser satisfechas. El Chicago Teachers Pension Fund, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Illinois, que gestionaba el seguro de salud del personal de Aspira, y una compañía prestamista llamada PEAC Solutions cada uno tienen más de $200,000 adeudados.</p><p>Edgar López, el director ejecutivo que se fue después del cierre de las escuelas de Aspira, cree que debe recibir $240,000, pero Aspira rechaza esa afirmación. López no respondió a los mensajes en busca de comentarios.</p><p>Aspira también debe más de $54,000 a ComEd y casi $26,000 a Peoples Gas.</p><p>En total, Aspira enumera $1.5 millones en deudas no garantizadas que no están respaldadas por propiedades u otras garantías.</p><p>Las CPS figuran en la lista de acreedores de Aspira presentada en los registros de la corte, pero, según los documentos de bancarrota, la deuda con el distrito escolar es sólo de alrededor de $2,700. El abogado del distrito escolar aún no se ha presentado ante la corte ni ha presentado una moción para intervenir.</p><p>La corte de bancarrota decidirá qué ocurre una vez que se paguen los acreedores de Aspira. Además de cualquier dinero que quede de la venta del edificio de Milwaukee Avenue, Aspira tiene el edificio de Barry Avenue y casi 800 artículos en inventario, incluidos numerosas computadoras portátiles, bocinas, microscopios y muebles escolares.</p><h3>Algunos dicen que la situación de Aspira apunta a la necesidad de más rendición de cuentas</h3><p>Ninguna otra escuela chárter se ha declarado en bancarrota en Chicago y es extremadamente raro que ocurra en cualquier lugar, aunque algunas cientos cierran cada año, según la National Alliance for Public Charter Schools, organización de defensa con sede en Washington D.C.</p><p>Derek W. Black, profesor de Derecho en la Universidad de Carolina del Sur que ha escrito extensamente sobre escuelas chárter, dice que mucha gente no entiende que las escuelas chárter reciben fondos públicos pero en gran medida se les deja administrar y gastar su dinero como quieran. Normalmente, dijo, sus activos “no pertenecen al pueblo del estado de Ohio o Illinois o Nueva Jersey”.</p><p>Y aunque algunos estados tienen medidas de rendición de cuentas que dictan qué sucede si una escuela chárter cierra, a menudo, cuando un operador se va, no hay mucho que les haga rendir cuentas.</p><p>Esto plantea preguntas como: “¿Quién protege a los contribuyentes?” dijo Black. “¿Quién protege a la comunidad?”.</p><p>López, el exdirector ejecutivo de Aspira, argumentó que la forma en que CPS financia a las escuelas chárter condujo a los problemas financieros de Aspira. Acusó a CPS de dar a las chárter sólo el 83% de lo que el distrito normalmente gastaría por estudiante, y no el 97% que exige la ley estatal.</p><p>Señaló que la organización estaba condenada por esa discrepancia, junto con una caída en las inscripciones y un aumento en los costos laborales por el personal sindicalizado.</p><p>The Illinois Network of Charter Schools, un grupo de defensa de las chárter, no defendió a Aspira, pero dijo en un comunicado que esperaba que se siguieran los procesos legales adecuados en el cierre de las escuelas chárter y en los procedimientos de bancarrota.</p><p>El grupo también reiteró su preocupación de que las chárter de Chicago están siendo subfinanciadas mientras enfrentan muchos de los mismos desafíos de inscripción y financieros que las escuelas administradas por el distrito.</p><p>Pero los funcionarios de CPS sostienen que las dificultades de Aspira son únicas.</p><p>En noviembre pasado, CPS le dijo a la junta de Aspira que una investigación del distrito que duró varios meses supuestamente encontró “una falla de gobernanza” y “una falta de la conocimiento financiero necesario para dirigir con éxito una escuela”.</p><p>Cuando López pidió un segundo adelanto de efectivo en febrero, la Junta Escolar de Chicago objetó y luego <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/03/20/cps-revoca-la-capacidad-de-aspira-para-operar-escuelas-charter-en-chicago" target="_blank" >votó por unanimidad en marzo</a> para terminar su contrato con Aspira, la única vez que el distrito escolar ha revocado una chárter en medio del año escolar.</p><p>WBEZ ha buscado información para obtener un panorama más claro de lo que condujo a los problemas financieros de Aspira. En marzo, WBEZ presentó una solicitud de Libertad de Información a Aspira para obtener información sobre nóminas, estados financieros, auditorías y otros registros públicos.</p><p>Las escuelas chárter están sujetas a la ley estatal de acceso a registros, pero Aspira no proporcionó los documentos solicitados. Chicago Public Media demandó a Aspira en la corte de circuito del Condado de Cook por acceso a esos documentos.</p><p>El abogado de bancarrota de Aspira, Paul Bach, ha sostenido que el caso de acceso a registros quedó automáticamente en suspenso debido a la presentación de la bancarrota. Pero los abogados de Chicago Public Media dijeron que apelarán esa decisión.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Man, 55, shot in Garfield Park neighborhood in June dies
entries.summary: <p>A man shot on the city's West Side in June died earlier this week from the wound, officials said. </p><p>A Monday autopsy determined David Allen, 55, died of complications of a gunshot wound and his death was ruled a homicide, according to the Cook County medical examiner's office. </p><p>Allen was in the 3400 block of West Van Buren Street when someone shot him on June 16, according to the medical examiner's office. </p><p>Allen, of the 6000 block of South Stony Island Avenue, was taken to the University of Illinois Hospital, where he died Sunday at 1:33 a.m., the medical examiner's office said. </p><p>No arrests were reported by police. </p><p>Area 4 detectives are investigating.<br></p>

entries.title: What to know after latest round of tornadoes tear through south suburbs
entries.summary: <p>As hundreds of thousands of Illinois and northwest Indiana residents remain without power following severe storms that brought at least three tornadoes to the area Tuesday, another threat of severe weather — with potentially twister-like winds — was moving through the area Wednesday. </p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/12/more-severe-storms-damaging-winds-may-hit-south-suburbs-over-142-000-still-without-power-in-chicago-area" target="_blank" >severe thunderstorm watch</a> was in effect for Joliet, Kankakee, DeKalb until 1 p.m., according to the National Weather Service. Severe weather could bring downpours and gusty winds, though the storms may not be as strong as Tuesday’s storms.</p><p>“Most areas are not gonna see severe winds, but if you do, you could see winds as high as 70 miles per hour,” Gino Izzi, a meteorologist with the weather service said.</p><p>Residents in Illinois and northwest Indiana were left reeling from Tuesday's storms, where <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/11/severe-weather-expected-in-chicago-area-and-other-areas-of-illinois" target="_blank" >t</a><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/11/severe-weather-expected-in-chicago-area-and-other-areas-of-illinois" target="_blank" >hree tornadoes with gusts of 86 to 110 mph</a> were confirmed Tuesday: One in southern Cook County, another in eastern Will County, and the third in the Mokena area, also in Will County.</p><p>In south suburban Mokena, where one of the three confirmed tornadoes hit, winds took down trees and cut power to many homes.</p><p>Rick Johnson, a Mokena resident of more than 30 years, said he’s never experienced so many powerful and destructive storms in a single summer.</p><p>“It’s been an odd year,” he said.</p><p>With more tornado-like conditions approaching the Chicago area and northwest Indiana, here's what you need to know. </p><h3><b>Why are there so many tornadoes in Illinois this year?</b></h3><p>So far this year, Illinois has experienced a record number of tornadoes.</p><p>Meteorologists say multiple rounds of severe weather this spring and summer have contributed to the elevated tornado count.</p><p>Illinois has already broken the state record for most tornadoes in a year. According to preliminary numbers from the National Weather Service, Illinois has recorded 198 tornadoes as of Aug. 11. The highest mark the state recorded before this year was 142 twisters in 2024.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Allen Cunningham/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>What should I do after a tornado alert?</b></h3><p>Illinois state climatologist Trent Ford said every Midwesterner should have the proper plans in place in the event of severe weather warnings in order to make sure family members are safe, together and know what to do. Things like going down into the basement, if you have one, and keeping your phone and other electronic items charged in case of outages. Also make sure to follow messaging from the National Weather Service.</p><p>Some residents admitted they, like Rob Griffin in Lansing, underestimated past storms despite emergency alerts being sent to cellphones and the blaring of tornado sirens.</p><p>“I think they’re doing a good job of warning us,” said Griffin, who lost nearly all of his roof during <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/28/storms-flooding-tornadoes-damage-worker-missing-power-outage" >late July’s severe storms</a>. “Hopefully, we, as citizens, will take heed to that.”</p><h3><b>Are tornadoes becoming more common in Illinois?</b></h3><p>While tornado activity can change from year to year, 2026’s activity has reached the highest point in recent years.</p><p>Still, it doesn’t mean Illinois is the new Tornado Alley. Yet.</p><p>According to some definitions, Illinois actually has been considered part of Tornado Alley for some time. Initially, the nickname applied to Southwestern states ravaged by twisters in the last century, such as Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas.</p><h3><b>Is climate change causing more tornadoes?</b></h3><p>The answer isn’t straightforward.</p><p>Ford previously told the Sun-Times warmer temperatures and increased moisture in the atmosphere can create environments that favor stronger thunderstorms.</p><p>However, researchers say the relationship between climate change and tornadoes themselves remains less certain.</p><p>Ford said a warmer, more humid climate may be contributing to more environments favorable for severe storms, though scientists are still studying exactly how those conditions affect tornado frequency.</p><p><i>Contributing: Mohammad Samra, Elijah James, Brett Chase</i></p>

entries.summary: <p>Nearly 41,000 White Sox fans <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/11/white-sox-pope-leo-hat-night" target="_blank" >gathered at Rate Field Tuesday</a> for a Pope Leo XIV-themed night featuring the stadiumwide giveaway of a pontiff-style Sox hat and a fifth-inning "peace be with you" greeting.</p><p>Before he became leader of the Catholic Church last year, Robert Francis Prevost was known to many as "Father Bob," a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/religion/2025/05/08/cardinal-robert-prevost-raised-in-dolton-is-the-first-american-pope" target="_blank" >Chicago-born</a> Sox fan who <a class="Link" players embraced the local legacy Tuesday, as Sister Mary Jo Sobieck of the Dominican Sisters of Springfield threw the first pitch while the team's Southpaw mascot donned his own pope hat and entries.title: In-season tourney schedule is out and NBA Cup could runneth over Bulls
entries.summary: <p>While the NBA was expected to announce the full team schedules on Thursday, they continued leaving breadcrumbs 24 hours earlier, releasing the in-season NBA Cup slate for 2026.</p><p>The Bulls already knew what the pool was – facing Atlanta, Washington, Boston and Charlotte in the Eastern Conference Group C – and now they know the when and where.</p><p>The team will host two Motorola Razr Cup Nights on Nov. 13 against the Hawks and Nov. 20 against the Wizards at the United Center, and will play the Celtics in Boston on Oct. 30 before travelling south to Charlotte to face the Hornets on Nov. 25.</p><p>Unfortunately for the new-look Bulls they will likely be the underdog in all four games.</p><p>Washington finished with an NBA-worst 17-65 record last season but are expected to take a huge leap with All-Stars Trae Young and Anthony Davis – both acquired last season – healthy and available to go along with No.1 pick AJ Dybantsa and a handful of other talented young players like Alex Sarr, Will Riley and Kyshawn George,</p><p>The Hornets added Naz Reid in a trade and Hannes Steinbach in the draft to join former Bull Coby White and talented lottery picks like Kon Knueppel and Brandon Miller.</p><p>Meanwhile, Atlanta and Boston are both eyeing playoff runs with enough talent to be top five teams in the conference.</p><p>Following group play, the tournament will move to knockout rounds for the remaining eight teams (three group winners and one wildcard from each conference) with the championship game played on Dec. 11 at the Hinkle Fieldhouse in Indianapolis.</p>
entries.author: Joe Cowley

entries.title: Russell Westbrook retires after 18 seasons in NBA
entries.summary: <p>SACRAMENTO, Calif. — Russell Westbrook, the NBA's career leader in triple-doubles and the 2017 MVP, announced Wednesday he's retiring after 18 seasons during which he was selected to the league's 75th anniversary team.</p><p>The two-time scoring champion shared his decision on social media in a post featuring a video narrated by actor Michael B. Jordan where the guard never says a word.</p><p>"Sometimes you don't even know when you've already watched the end," Westbrook wrote. "You had to be there. And now it's over."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Sometimes you don’t even know when you’ve already watched the end.<br><br>You had to be there. And now it’s over. <a href="https://t.co/6YoOW8WyIV">pic.twitter.com/6YoOW8WyIV</a></p>— Russell Westbrook (@russwest44) <a href="https://x.com/russwest44/status/2087607645540585686?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 12, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Westbrook was the No. 4 pick in 2008 out of UCLA by the Seattle SuperSonics, just before they moved to Oklahoma City. He played his first 11 seasons with the Thunder and spent this past season with the Sacramento Kings.</p><p>Westbrook led the NBA in assists three times and was a two-time MVP of the All-Star Game. He won an Olympic gold medal in the 2012 London Games.</p><p>Westbrook leaves with 209 triple-doubles, the last on March 15. Nikola Jokic ranks second in that category with 198 going into this season. Westbrook also holds the NBA mark for most triple-doubles in a season with 42 in 2016-17, when he earned his only MVP award.</p><p>He averaged double figures for points and assists in five of six seasons starting in the 2015-16 season.</p><p>Westbrook also played for Houston, Washington, the Lakers and Clippers — splitting the 2022-23 season between the Los Angeles teams and Denver.</p><p>Last season, Westbrook started 58 of the 64 games he played for Sacramento. He averaged 15.2 points and 6.7 assists.<br></p>

entries.title: CTA deploying violence interrupters, mental health clinicians on trains this fall
entries.summary: <p>Dozens of non-law enforcement personnel trained to intervene in violence and mental health crises are expected to start riding trains this fall on the CTA Red, Blue and Green lines.</p><p>The Chicago Transit Authority board on Wednesday approved a $10 million, yearlong Crisis Intervention Safe Ride Specialist Pilot designed to complement the recent boost in security and police on trains and buses.</p><p>The specialists, drawn from contracts with four local groups, will don colorful vests while they provide mental, behavioral, and drug-use treatment services to those who need it, Nora Leerhsen, the CTA's acting president, told the board.</p><p>The largest of the four contracts, worth $6.6 million, goes to Metropolitan Family Services, the group that performs community violence intervention across the city. That group will provide 20 daily community violence intervention specialists on the Red Line, 7 days a week from Roosevelt to Lake Street in two shifts spanning from noon to 3:30 a.m., CTA's chief of security, Joe Bird, told board members.</p><p>Leerhsen said the pilot program was timed on purpose to complement the agency's "multi-layered security strategy" that included adding more cops and sheriff's deputies, helping <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/07/08/cta-transit-crime-security-surge" target="_blank" >drive a 30% decline in crime</a> over last year.</p><p>These new non-police personnel will help unload some of the work that has recently been addressed by police, she said.</p><p>"This is an incredibly historic moment to launch these programs ... following months of increased law enforcement ... doing things that are frankly not in their job description," Leerhsen said.</p><p>The remaining three contracts went to groups that will supply mental health, homelessness and substance abuse recovery intervention specialists to the Green and Blue lines.</p><p>One of those groups, Maywood-based Housing Forward, has a nearly $1 million deal to provide specialists on the Green Line from Harlem to Central Avenue, Molly Poppe, CTA's chief innovation officer, told the board. They will be staffed Monday to Friday from 6 p.m. to 1 a.m., and on Saturdays from 6 p.m. to 11:30 p.m., she said.</p><p>Healthcare Alternative Systems will supply bilingual behavioral health care to the Blue Line's northwest branch, from O'Hare to Logan Square, Poppe said. Two teams of two to three people will service those trains from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday to Friday.</p><p>The fourth group, Street Samaritans, has a $1.2 million contract to supply two three-person teams on the Blue Line's western branch, from Austin to Forest Park, Poppe said. Each team will have one licensed mental health clinician and two crisis intervention specialists trained in de-escalation.</p><p>This is the first time the CTA has officially employed violence interrupters, not counting the unsanctioned Violence Interrupters, led by Tio Hardiman, who have <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/4/20/23033981/cta-crime-violence-interrupters-volunteer-security-guards-red-line" target="_blank" >patrolled</a> the southern branch of the Red Line.</p><p>Some members of the CTA board, which will be <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/06/01/nita-rta-transit-law-cta-metra-pace" target="_blank" >replaced next month by Northern Illinois Transit Authority board appointments</a>, questioned how the violence interrupters would be trained to either call or not call police for backup.</p><p>"Their first goal ... is de-escalation... and offer resources," Bird said. "When it rises to criminal activity, the threat of violence, then 911 and police should be notified. But not before that. They should act independently."</p><p>A CTA spokesman said the specialists are expected to be deployed by the fall.</p>

entries.title: Bears coach Ben Johnson softens his tone as QB Caleb Williams no longer 'drowning' in offense
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" >Caleb Williams</a> could write a book about the misadventures of his first two training camps, and a tell-all on that would be riveting.</p><p>First there was his rookie onboarding, which would be a scramble for anyone, but even more so under former coach Matt Eberflus, then the relentless deluge of information and criticism from Ben Johnson in their first camp together. The latter was such an intense experience that Williams described it as “drowning.”</p><p>Camp has been just as strenuous this year — Johnson has no let-up, ever — but Williams is more at ease with it.</p><p>He still has ample work to do and much to prove, particularly as a consistent, efficient passer, but this part of the process is more comfortable. He accepts that there will be great days and bad ones — neither of which should make him overreact.</p><p>“I’m head above water,” he said, laughing to himself.</p><p>It helps to have a firm handle on what Johnson wants, and Johnson said Williams has been able to identify his mistakes without needing them pointed out. That’s the first step toward making fewer of them, and the real test of that won’t come until the opener Sept. 13 at the Panthers.</p><p>In the meantime, Williams is unlikely to play in the first preseason game Saturday against the Browns. He should get extensive work in a joint practice with the Bengals next week and the Titans the week after, but whether he plays in preseason games against those teams likely hinges on how sharp the offense looks in practice.</p><p>Johnson has been pleased overall, but seems like he might be on the brink of turning up the heat after seeing a “plateau” this week.</p><p>It’s a sign of growth in their relationship that Williams wasn’t bothered by that feedback. The tediousness of training camp requires him to have “that mental fortitude” to maintain focus throughout and remain undeterred by setbacks.</p><p>“I've gotten better with that,” Williams said. “Just being able to encourage myself, being able to get out of those funks.”</p><p>All of it, while far from a finished product, is coming together more smoothly than it did last August. Johnson was perpetually frustrated with the offense, and its sloppiness spilled into the regular season.</p><p>Johnson believed his confrontational, unfiltered style was a “shock to the system” in his first training camp with Williams, and that’s not surprising given the more understated and even timid, at times, approach by Eberflus and former offensive coordinator Shane Waldron.</p><p>While those two seemed deferential to Williams, Johnson coached him like a rookie. He’s still doing a version of that because the fact remains that Williams is young, unproven and has lagged in some of the basic elements of quarterback play, but it’s more collaborative and less like scolding.</p><p>“There’s still a level of detail and we’re certainly very demanding of him, yet when I see the progress being made... I haven’t been quite as stern with my delivery,” Johnson told the Sun-Times. “When you see [players’] commitment coming into the building every day, studying the playbook, knowing their assignments, you don’t have to be as hard on them.”</p><p>That affirmation carries a more weight than when previous coaches touted supposed progress on the practice fields at Halas Hall. Those coaches still hesitated about Mitch Trubisky and Justin Fields at times, and Johnson has earned some credibility by refusing to sugarcoat anything publicly.</p><p>He also comes to work every day with wild ambition, and he wouldn’t tolerate anything short of total commitment from Williams to those same goals. Johnson doesn’t merely want to win. He wants to be overwhelming.</p><p>“[Everyone says their] goal is to win the Super Bowl; I want more than that,” Johnson said in an interview with The Athletic. “I want to have the highest-scoring offense ever, which happens to be the 2013 Denver Broncos.</p><p>“I want to surpass them. I want shutouts. I want blowouts.”</p><p>Those Broncos averaged 37.9 points per game, though they lost Super Bowl XLVIII to the Seahawks. The Bears were ninth in the league at 25.9 last season, so there’s a lot of ground to cover. Developing Williams into a complete quarterback and not just a highlight machine is the key to chasing that record.</p><p>Johnson isn’t going to back off that any more than he’s going to with his mandate that Williams completes 70% of his passes. It’s not a suggestion.</p><p>That starts now, and everything about Williams’ preparation has improved since the Bears hired Johnson, as well as signing longtime backup quarterback Case Keenum to serve as a mentor. He’s no longer “drowning” while trying to catch up to Johnson’s offense and has the bandwidth to focus on refining his routine.</p><p>“My process is better,” Williams said, listing off everything from what he eats before practice to how to be prepared for meetings and walk-throughs. “Being able to be in control of that, know my own schedule, know what's going on, and then just knowing the offense and being more detailed about it has helped me tremendously.”</p><p>Those are tiny steps, but they’re the only ones he can take at the moment with the season far in the distance. The Bears’ hope is that he takes enough of them between now and then to make a meaningful, noticeable difference when the real games resume.</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module entries.title: Bears coach Ben Johnson eyes NFL's scoring record
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach Ben Johnson is never shy about setting lofty goals.</p><p>His target for scoring this year: the 2013 Peyton Manning-led Broncos, who scored an NFL-record 37.9 points per game.</p><p>“I know how many points they scored and I want to surpass them,” he told The Athletic in a story published Wednesday. “I want shutouts. I want blowouts.”</p><p>Johnson also said that he wants to surpass the NFL’s record for consecutive wins — and to post an undefeated season. He said he wants Bears players to embrace those targets as though they’re within reach.</p><p>The Bears finished ninth in the NFL with 25.9 points per game last year. Reaching the Broncos’ record would take an extra 12.1 points per game. The 1941 Bears hold the franchise record for most points per game, with 36.</p><p>At their peak last year, the Bears won five games in a row. entries.title: Bally's is using battle over video gambling as excuse to slow construction at casino site, aldermen say
entries.summary: <p>A City Council majority on Wednesday accused Bally’s of using the ongoing battle over video gambling terminals in Chicago as an excuse to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/09/ballys-to-stop-work-on-some-amenities-at-permanent-chicago-casino-development-amid-video-gambling-dispute" >slow down construction</a> of a $1.7 billion casino and entertainment complex in River West that they contend Bally's can no longer afford to build.</p><p>The letter to Bally's was signed by 28 members of the renegade coalition that rejected Mayor Brandon Johnson’s corporate head tax and muscled through an alternative 2026 budget. That spending plan lifted the Chicago ban on video gambling, and assumed the city would generate $6.8 million by licensing newly legalized <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/09/16/video-gaming-in-chicago-proposal-anthony-beale-brandon-johnson" target="_blank" >video gambling terminals</a>.</p><p>It claims the company's unilateral decision to pause construction of “all non-gaming elements” of the casino complex — including the hotel, event center and some restaurants — is a violation of the company’s host agreement with the city.</p><p>The letter demands that Johnson enforce the agreement and ensure that Bally’s "delivers the complete project it committed to build.” </p><p>If Johnson refuses, the City Council majority says it will do it for him — by summoning Bally’s executives to a public hearing and perhaps filing a lawsuit against the gambling giant.</p><p>Legal action by the city would turn the tables on Bally’s, whose executives have threatened to sue the city and cancel its $4 million a year lump-sum payment to Chicago taxpayers in response to the City Council's authorization of video gambling terminals, which Bally's says violates the company’s host agreement.</p><p>“Final completion… expressly depends upon substantial completion of the hotel, retail, event space, exhibition space, greenspace, Riverwalk and other components — not merely the gaming floor,” the letter states.</p><p>“Continuing construction of the casino floor while slowing the hotel and other non-gaming portions does not eliminate those obligations” and constitutes a “material change” to the contract that requires City Council approval, the Council majority wrote.</p><p>Bally's responded with a statement saying it understands its host agreement obligations and is ready to explain to the Council its reasons for slowing down the project. </p><p>"We have held up, and will hold up, our end of the bargain," Bally's stated. "We look forward to stating our case that VGTs will not benefit the City the way it has been represented, especially if their rollout will cause material detriment to our business." </p><p></p><p></p><p>The $1.7 billion casino project has encountered financial and logistical challenges since Bally’s was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/5/25/23141244/ballys-casino-approved-chicago-city-council-river-west-medinah-temple-lightfoot-police-fire-pensions" target="_blank" >selected</a> to build Chicago’s casino in 2022, including an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/casinos-gambling/2024/03/12/ballys-chicago-casino-buyout-soo-kim" target="_blank" >$800 million</a> “funding gap,” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2024/1/22/24047289/ballys-casino-hotel-tower-plans-changes-city-hall-chicago-river" target="_blank" >changes to its hotel plans</a> and delays that pushed the permanent casino’s expected opening into 2027.</p><p>Downtown Ald. Brendan Reilly (42nd) said not a single video gambling license has been issued by the city, and there has been no impact on Bally’s bottom line.</p><p>“Many of us suspect that this is really a cash-flow issue for Bally’s and they’re trying to turn lemons into lemonade by blaming VGT as the reason they’re slowing down construction,” Reilly said. “They’ve told their own investors that they are heavily leveraged and have over $5 billion in debt, and that encumbrance could have a negative impact on their future operations.” </p><p>Ald. Anthony Beale (9th), who's been leading the charge to legalize video gambling terminals, agreed with Reilly.</p><p>"We believe they don't have the cash flow and they're blaming VGTs that are not even operational in the city of Chicago," Beale said. "We need to get to the bottom of what is really going on... If they cannot fulfill their obligation to the city, we need to be looking for another operator."</p><p>Bally’s has warned repeatedly that lifting Chicago’s ban on video gambling would cost the city $74 million in annual revenue and up to 1,050 jobs at its temporary and permanent casinos.</p><p>The casino giant has further warned that lifting the ban would force the Johnson administration to renegotiate “critical elements” of its host agreement, wipe out a yearly $4 million lump-sum payment from Bally’s, and shrink the casino jackpot needed to save police and fire pension funds.</p><p>Johnson has raised strong objections to legalizing video gambling and lobbied alderpersons to repeal the authorization. But Reilly argued that Johnson has an obligation to enforce the host agreement. </p><p>“A deal’s a deal. They can’t play these games when taxpayers and police [officers] and firefighters are counting on these revenues to support their pensions. It’s cheap gamesmanship,” Reilly said.</p><p>Ald. Walter R. Burnett (27th), whose ward includes the permanent casino complex, said he's frustrated by the slowdown, but believes Bally's is operating within its legal rights.</p><p>"If you assume that your revenue is going to go down to nothing, you want to re-evaluate the cost before you have to commit everything to it," Burnett said.</p><p></p><p>The mayor's office had no immediate comment on the letter.</p>

entries.title: Colleges scramble after court strikes down in-state tuition for Illinois undocumented students
entries.summary: <p>Thousands of immigrant students who attended high school in Illinois may soon have to pay more expensive out-of-state tuition rates for college — a change that could jeopardize their access to higher education.</p><p>On July 24 a federal judge appointed by President Donald Trump <a class="Link" href="https://npr.brightspotcdn.com/2b/57/27b24572418b89ce553d526f2a18/gov-uscourts-ilsd-106533-49-0.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>struck down parts of three Illinois laws</u></a> that allowed eligible undocumented students to pay in-state tuition rates at community colleges and public universities and to receive state financial aid.</p><p>Judge David Dugan of the Southern District of Illinois sided with the U.S. Department of Justice in its argument that these provisions violate federal law because they grant a benefit to non-citizens who live in state that citizens who live out of state cannot get.</p><p>The state law <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocNum=60&GAID=3&DocTypeID=HB&LegId=195&SessionID=3&GA=93" target="_blank" ><u>concerning in-state tuition</u></a> had been on the books for more than two decades. To qualify for the benefit, students must have attended an Illinois high school for at least three years, among other criteria.</p><p>Dugan paused the implementation of the ruling for two weeks to allow state officials time to appeal, but it is unclear if they will do so. Immigrant rights groups like the Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights worry an appeal could overturn in-state tuition policies for undocumented students across the country. Already, Illinois State University, one of the defendants in the case, has decided not to challenge the decision, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wglt.org/local-news/2026-08-05/federal-court-blocks-in-state-tuition-rates-and-financial-aid-for-undocumented-college-students-in-illinois" target="_blank" ><u>WGLT reported</u></a>.</p><p>The Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights estimates that 7,000 to 10,000 undocumented students “could lose vital educational support for the upcoming academic year as a direct result of this ruling,” the organization’s deputy director, Veronica Castro, said in a statement. “Families will have to make difficult financial decisions and enrollment rates may take a hit, which is a huge setback for our communities.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" The organization estimates that 7,000 to 10,000 undocumented students could lose support in the upcoming school year due to the federal court ruling.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Peggy Heinrich, president of Elgin Community College, said the ruling removes “a critical source of aid” that's allowed undocumented students “to receive education and become productive, contributing members in our society.”</p><p>The community college is a federally designated Hispanic Serving Institution and more than half of its students identify as Hispanic or Latino.</p><p>Heinrich said her college and others across Illinois are looking to state officials for guidance about what the ruling means.</p><p>“We have to comply, so we are trying to do the best we can to make sure our students understand what resources may be available to them, or what we can do in terms of our college’s payment plan options,” Heinrich said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.higheredimmigrationportal.org/state/illinois/" target="_blank" ><u>Nearly 25,000 students</u></a> at colleges and universities in Illinois are undocumented, according to the Higher Ed Immigration Portal, which tracks immigrant student enrollment data across the country.</p><p>At many colleges, the difference between in-state and out-of-state tuition is substantial. At the University of Illinois Chicago, <a class="Link" href="https://uofi.app.box.com/s/3ub3lw8qeda73k7u9bl2927o66vhyvzq" target="_blank" ><u>out-of-state tuition is nearly triple</u></a> the price of in-state tuition for full-time undergraduate students.</p><p>The University of Illinois System, which oversees UIC, the University of Illinois Springfield and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, <a class="Link" href="https://today.uic.edu/important-update-regarding-recent-federal-court-ruling/" target="_blank" ><u>told students in an email on Aug. 3</u></a> that university administrators are working with state officials and lawyers to assess the implications of the ruling.</p><p>“Our immediate priority is to provide accurate information and offer timely guidance and support as additional details become available,” administrators wrote.</p><p>Already, the application that undocumented students across Illinois would have submitted to receive state financial aid, known as the Alternative Application for Illinois Financial Aid, is no longer available.</p><p>“This means that students who have submitted or planned to submit the 2026-27 Alternative Application, such as Illinois undocumented students, cannot be considered for this program for the 2026-27 school year,” a <a class="Link" href="https://www.isac.org/students/during-college/types-of-financial-aid/grants/monetary-award-program/" target="_blank" ><u>notice about the ruling</u></a> from the Illinois Student Assistance Commission reads.</p><p>An estimated 2,150 undocumented students received state financial aid through one of the agency’s programs for the 2025-2026 school year, a spokesperson said. That includes MAP grants for students with low income.</p><p>The Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights advised students to save copies of their financial aid award letters, tuition bills and communication from their college or university and to consult with their academic advisors or financial aid or admissions officers.</p><p>The organization is hosting an information session for students and families about the ruling <a class="Link" href="http://facebook.com/ICIRR/" target="_blank" ><u>on Facebook Live</u></a> at 5:30 pm on Wednesday, Aug. 12 in collaboration with the Latino Policy Forum.</p><p><i>Lisa Kurian Philip covers higher education for WBEZ in partnership with</i> <a class="Link" href="https://www.opencampusmedia.org/" target="_blank" ><i>Open Campus</i></a><i>.</i></p>

entries.title: ICE agent pleads guilty to off-duty attack at Brookfield gas station
entries.summary: <p>A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent pleaded guilty Wednesday to an off-duty attack late last year at a gas station in west suburban Brookfield. </p><p>Adam Saracco, 41, was sentenced to a year of court supervision on a single misdemeanor count of battery during a brief hearing before Cook County Circuit Judge Owens J. Shelby.</p><p>Saracco was charged earlier this year after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/01/23/ice-officer-charged-with-attacking-immigrant-rights-activist-in-chicago-suburbs" target="_blank" >attacking attorney and activist Robert Held</a> on Dec. 27. Held followed Saracco from the ICE processing facility in Broadview and filmed him as he stopped at a gas station in the 9200 block of East 31st Street in Brookfield. Held said Saracco eventually approached him and pushed him to the ground.</p><p>“I’m gratified that there is some accountability," Held told the Sun-Times. "But as a country we have a long way to go."</p><p>Held pushed for the Cook County state’s attorney’s office to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/26/ice-midway-blitz-adam-saracco-robert-held-trump-chicago-brookfield" target="_blank" >upgrade Saracco’s case</a> to a felony matter, but prosecutors refused. </p><p>Held argued that Saracco should face a felony charge because the alleged attack occurred on a public sidewalk and Held is over 60. But prosecutors said a felony charge would require them to prove Saracco knew Held was over 60 and noted they rarely pursue aggravated battery charges based solely on the location of an alleged attack.</p><p>Saracco's attorney couldn't be reached. Neither could ICE.</p><p>Saracco’s conviction comes amid continued calls to hold federal agents accountable for their actions during Operation Midway Blitz, the Trump administration's deportation campaign in the Chicago area last fall. On Monday, residents marched into the Chicago Police Department’s Area 3 headquarters in North Center to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/08/10/marimar-martinez-others-file-police-reports-against-midway-blitz-agents-in-new-push-for-accountability" target="_blank" >report alleged crimes</a> involving immigration agents.</p><p>Cook County Circuit Judge Erica Reddick rejected a petition to appoint a special prosecutor to probe for criminal misconduct and potentially prosecute federal agents. The state’s attorney’s office has maintained that law enforcement agencies must investigate alleged crimes and present cases to prosecutors for charging.</p><p>No federal agents have been charged with an on-duty crime connected to Midway Blitz.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/01/23/ice-officer-charged-with-attacking-immigrant-rights-activist-in-chicago-suburbs" target="_blank" >ICE officer charged with attacking immigrant rights activist in Chicago suburb</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/26/ice-midway-blitz-adam-saracco-robert-held-trump-chicago-brookfield" target="_blank" >Attorney accusing ICE agent of suburban Chicago attack now pushing for felony charges</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/08/10/marimar-martinez-others-file-police-reports-against-midway-blitz-agents-in-new-push-for-accountability" target="_blank" >Marimar Martinez, others file police reports against Midway Blitz agents in new push for ICE accountability</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: El receptor Drew Romo se queda con los White Sox por su preparación y su trabajo con los pitchers
entries.summary: <p>Los <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> se han visto obligados a hacer varios cambios en la receptoría por lesiones esta temporada, pero desde que fue ascendido el 25 de abril, Drew Romo no ha sido uno de ellos.</p><p>Los aficionados miran su promedio de bateo de .126 al comenzar el martes y se preguntan por qué. Así que un periodista intrépido le preguntó a Romo, lo más educadamente posible, qué lo hace bueno.</p><p>“¿Por qué estoy aquí?”, respondió.</p><p>Ya que lo mencionó, sí. ¿Qué dirías que haces aquí?</p><p>“Diría que lo más importante es que he hecho un gran trabajo con los lanzadores”, dijo Romo. “De verdad aprendí en mis últimos años en el béisbol profesional con los informes de scouting, atacar a los bateadores, la secuencia de lanzamientos, la planificación del juego, poder tener una comunicación clara con el cuerpo técnico, los lanzadores, los compañeros”.</p><p>Pero él sabe lo que ven los aficionados.</p><p>“Obviamente no estoy bateando bien ahora mismo”, compartió. “Pero ahora me importa más ganar juegos y, después de eso, las efectividades (ERA) de mis lanzadores y no permitir carreras. Eso para mí es lo más importante”.</p><p>Los Sox reclamaron a Romo, de 24 años, de los Mets vía waivers en enero y lo enviaron a Triple-A Charlotte. Tras empezar la temporada con Reese McGuire como su segundo receptor, los Sox lo cortaron y subieron a Romo, quien se ha ganado la confianza de los lanzadores y entrenadores.</p><p>“Él maneja el juego tan bien”, dijo el zurdo Anthony Kay, que lanzó seis entradas con dos carreras en la victoria del sábado contra los Guardians con Romo detrás del plato. “Se ve el trabajo que hace antes del partido. La comunicación entre entradas también es enorme. Si quieres que haga algo diferente, escucha y capta de inmediato. Tener una comunicación abierta en ambos sentidos es lo que construye esa relación y esa confianza”.</p><p>Hablando del sábado, Walker McKinven, entrenador de banquillo de los Sox, que también hace las veces de entrenador de receptores, dijo que Romo posiblemente tuvo uno de los mejores juegos defensivos que un jugador de los Sox ha tenido en toda la temporada.</p><p>“Tuvo un juego de recepción muy, muy positivo”, comentó McKinven. “Hizo esa gran jugada en el squeeze de seguridad; eliminó a un corredor. Realmente fue un partido enorme y discreto, a pesar de lo que pasó en el otro lado del béisbol. Le atribuyo gran parte de la victoria a Drew. Manejó bien a Anthony. Hizo ajustes cuando fue necesario. Cualquier cosa que vea y ajuste sobre la marcha es porque está bien preparado”.</p><p>Ese trabajo mantiene a Romo con los Sox, quizá incluso para los playoffs, cuando el pitcheo y la defensa pueden decidir los partidos.</p><p>“Mediblemente, le va bien en lo que valoramos, y eso realmente está sosteniendo su valor agregado”, dijo McKinven. “Trabaja muy duro en su recepción, su tiro, en prepararse para las corridas de los rivales. Es realmente un tipo bien preparado, orgulloso de la posición y de lo que se requiere en ese puesto. Es un gran compañero de equipo y eso vale mucho cuando un receptor se gana la confianza de la gente”.</p><p>Los aficionados a menudo pueden ver a un lanzador de los Sox, como Kay el sábado, señalar enfáticamente hacia Romo, y viceversa, después de un ponche. Pero Romo todavía trabaja en ciertos aspectos de la receptoría, como enmarcar el lanzamiento.</p><p>“El valor de las carreras del framing es lo más importante”, dijo. “Y también mi tiro: he cometido algunos errores recientemente. Así que asegurarme de estar en la posición correcta para hacer un lanzamiento preciso, trabajar en lanzar desde diferentes posiciones”.</p><p>Romo también sigue trabajando en su bateo. Tras conectar cinco jonrones y registrar un OPS de .857 en sus primeros 17 juegos, no ha conectado jonrones y tiene un OPS de .252 en sus últimos 30.</p><p>“Hemos estado trabajando en tantas cosas buenas”, dijo Romo. “Todo lo que practicamos en la jaula y en los entrenamientos es excelente. Y luego, en el juego, simplemente no se ha conectado y es muy raro. Pero me alegra haber podido contribuir a la defensa. Esa es mi contribución a este equipo; así ayudo a ganar juegos. Así que estoy orgulloso de eso”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Speeding motorist dies after plowing into empty school bus in Humboldt Park: police
entries.summary: <p>A motorist was killed when he slammed into an empty school bus, causing a chain reaction collision late Tuesday in the Humboldt Park neighborhood. </p><p>About 10:55 p.m. in the 2700 block of West Augusta Boulevard a male driving a grey car at a high rate of speed slammed into a parked, empty school bus, police said. </p><p>That caused the bus to then crash into four unoccupied parked cars along the block, police said. </p><p>The driver was dead at the scene, according to police. </p><p>The Major Accident Investigation Unit is investigating.<br></p>
